name: Kerma
why: Wikipedia 'Kerma': 'Kerma was the capital city of the Kingdom of Kerma, which had its roots in the pre-Kerma culture ... from 3500 BC'; 'A state society formed between 2550 BC and 1550 BC'. Kingdom of Kerma ended with Egyptian New Kingdom conquest c. 1500 BC (general knowledge, approx).

name: Napata
why: Wikipedia 'Napata': 'founded by Thutmose III in the 15th century BC'; capital of Kushite Twenty-fifth Dynasty and then Kingdom of Kush; 'Napata finally lost its symbolic significance as the location of royal burials to Meroe' c. 270 BC. Exact date of final decline as a town not stated; 'to' approximated to when it lost primacy.

name: Meroë
why: Wikipedia 'Meroë': 'the capital of the Kingdom of Kush for several centuries from around 590 BC, until its collapse in the 4th century AD'.

name: Old Dongola
why: Wikipedia 'Old Dongola': founded 'in the fifth century as a fortress'; capital of Makuria from the mid-sixth century; 'the city's heyday was in the ninth-eleventh centuries, but building activity lasted until the fourteenth century'; 'during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries the town was in decline'; urban centre moved downstream to modern Dongola in the 19th century.

name: Soba
why: Wikipedia 'Soba (city)': 'the capital of the medieval Nubian kingdom of Alodia from the sixth century until around 1500'; 'the abandoned city was plundered for building material when Khartoum was founded in 1821'.

name: Faras
why: Wikipedia 'Faras': ancient Pachoras/Pakhoras; 'reached its height during the Christian period of Nubia, when Pakhoras was the capital of ... Nobadia'; wall paintings dated '8th to 14th century'; site now submerged under Lake Nasser. Precise foundation/abandonment dates not given by Wikipedia; approximated to the Nubian medieval decline.

name: Qasr Ibrim
why: Wikipedia 'Qasr Ibrim': 'a long history of occupation, ranging from as early as the eighth century BC to AD 1813'; 'occupied until 1813, when the last occupants were driven out by artillery fire'.

name: Meinarti
why: Wikipedia 'Meinarti': occupation Phase 1 began c. 30 BC; 'the final abandonment of Meinarti as a Nubian settlement undoubtedly coincided with the end of Christian Nubian civilization, around AD 1500'. Occupation was intermittent across several phases (approx).

name: Wad ban Naqa
why: Wikipedia 'Wad ban Naqa': palace 'built by Queen Amanishakheto (first century AD)'; part of the Kingdom of Kush near Meroë. No abandonment date given by Wikipedia; 'to' approximated to the general collapse of the Meroitic kingdom in the 4th century AD (general knowledge).

name: Kawa
why: Wikipedia 'Kawa, Sudan': known as 'Gematon' in ancient Egyptian texts, 'Patigga or Patinga during Greco-Roman times'; site of Egyptian New Kingdom and later Napatan/Meroitic temples. Precise settlement span not given by Wikipedia; dates approximated from the temple-building periods (general knowledge).

name: Suakin
why: Wikipedia 'Suakin': 'first mentioned by name in the 10th century by al-Hamdani, who says it was already an ancient town'; Red Sea port that declined after the Ottoman-Portuguese era and 'fell into ruin', but the settlement continues today, secondary to Port Sudan.

name: Sennar
why: Wikipedia 'Sennar (city)': the Funj 'made Sennar their capital' after overthrowing Alwa; the Funj Sultanate is conventionally dated from 1504. This falls right at the brief's 'about 1500' threshold; included as a judgement call. Sennar continues today as a city in Sudan.

name: Yeha
why: Wikipedia 'Yeha': 'likely served as the capital of the pre-Aksumite kingdom of D'mt'; temple 'dated ... to around 700 BC'. D'mt's rise is conventionally placed c. 10th century BC (general knowledge, approx). Yeha continues today as a town in Tigray.

name: Adulis
why: Wikipedia 'Adulis': pre-Aksumite settlement traces from the 'mid-2nd to early 1st millennium BCE'; major Red Sea port of Aksum; 'the naval power of Axum waned and the port of Adulis was abandoned sometime around the 8th century AD'.

name: Matara
why: Wikipedia 'Matara, Eritrea' (also 'Metera'): 'a major city in the D'mt and Aksumite kingdoms'; 'topmost layers are associated with the Aksumite Empire and date from the fourth to the eighth centuries'. Described as 'a small town' today, i.e. it continues.

name: Qohaito
why: Wikipedia 'Qohaito': pre-Aksumite settlement identified with 'Koloe' of the Periplus; 'the town is known to have survived to the sixth century AD'.

name: Aksum
why: Wikipedia 'Axum': 'by the 1st century AD, Aksum was described as a metropolis in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea'; capital of the Aksumite Empire; 'by the end of the 9th century, Aksum was largely abandoned and lay in ruins' as a political capital but revived as a religious centre and continues today as a town of 66,900 people.

name: Harar
why: Wikipedia 'Harar': 'various dates have been suggested, some state the city was founded by Qurayshi settlers in the late 7th century or a local creation in the 10th century'; made capital of the Adal Sultanate in 1520; continues today as a major Ethiopian city.

name: Lalibela
why: Wikipedia 'Lalibela': 'traditionally known as Roha, was founded during the Zagwe dynasty under the rule of King Gebre Meskel Lalibela'; rock churches carved 12th-14th centuries. Reign dates for Gebre Meskel Lalibela are disputed; approximated. Continues today as a town and UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Zeila
why: Wikipedia 'Zeila': 'most modern scholars identify it with the site of Avalites' (Avalites re-established 'at the end of the 1st century BCE' per the Avalites article); 'by the 9th century, Zeila was the capital of the early Adal Kingdom'; still a small port town in Somaliland today.

name: Berbera
why: Wikipedia 'Berbera': 'believed to be the ancient port of Malao ... described in the eighth chapter of the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea'; Malao's own article notes its 're-establishment took place at the end of the 1st century BCE'. Berbera continues today as a major Somaliland port.

name: Ras Hafun
why: Wikipedia 'Opone': ancient port 'identified with the city of Hafun through archaeological remains'; active '1st century BC and ... 3rd to 5th centuries AD'; 'as early as 50 AD, it was well known as a center for the cinnamon trade'. Modern Ras Hafun is a small settlement; rename year is a general-knowledge estimate.

name: Garama
why: Wikipedia 'Germa': 'known in ancient times as Garama', capital of the Garamantian Kingdom in the Fezzan; 'Garamantian power climaxed during the second and the third centuries AD'; captured by Rome in 203 and, per some sources, by Uqba ibn Nafi in 669 AD. Founding date of the Garamantian kingdom (c. 1st millennium BC) is general knowledge, approx. Modern Germa exists at/near the site today.

name: Sirwah
why: Wikipedia 'Sirwah': 'after Ma'rib, the most important economical and political center of the Kingdom of Saba at the beginning of the 1st century BC'; temple built 'about the year 700 BC'; lost its position as capital to Ma'rib.

name: Zafar
why: Wikipedia 'Zafar, Yemen': 'the capital of the Himyarites (110 BCE - 525 CE)'; 'Sana'a and its fortress Ghumdan replaced Zafar as capital probably between 537 and 548'; settlement 'declined drastically in the 5th and 6th centuries'.

name: Shabwa
why: Wikipedia 'Shabwa': 'the capital of the Kingdom of Hadhramaut'; 'first settled in 13th century BC, and was destroyed by the Himyarites at the end of the 3rd century AD'.

name: Shibam
why: Wikipedia 'Shibam': 'founded around the 3rd century and became the capital of the Kingdom of Hadhramaut in 300 AD, after the destruction of its previous capital, Shabwa'. Continues today as an inhabited UNESCO World Heritage town.

name: Sumhuram
why: Wikipedia 'Khor Rori': the port city of Sumhuram 'was founded in the 3rd century BC as an outpost for the Kingdom of Hadramawt'; 'it was finally abandoned in the 5th century, most likely due to the formation of the sandbar blocking the estuary'.

name: Najran
why: Wikipedia 'Najran': 'in the early 1st millennium BC, Najran was controlled by a commune called Muhamirum'; continuously inhabited since; a major modern Saudi city (population 381,431 in 2022) not yet shown in the atlas.

name: Dumat al-Jandal
why: Wikipedia 'Dumat al-Jandal': 'the city has a history dating back to the 10th century BC and is mentioned in Akkadian inscriptions ... in which it is referred to as Adummatu and is described as the capital of an Arab kingdom'. The modern town of Dumat al-Jandal continues at the site.

name: Tayma
why: Wikipedia 'Tayma': 'a substantial expansion of the settlement has been documented in the mid-2nd millennium BC'; long history as a major oasis, mentioned by the Assyrians in the 8th century BC; continues today as a Saudi town and governorate.

name: Qaryat al-Faw
why: Wikipedia 'Qaryat al-Faw': 'once the capital of the Kingdom of Kinda'; 'the city emerged in the fourth century BC, and flourished from the 3rd century BC until the 3rd century AD'; 'the Kinda abandoned it around 300 AD to settle in Hadhramaut'.

name: Dedan
why: Wikipedia 'Lihyan': capital of the Dadanite/Lihyanite kingdoms, at the Al-'Ula oasis; 'the term Dedanite usually describes the earlier phase ... since their capital name was Dedan'; 'the Lihyanites ... appeared in the 4th century BC and disappeared in the 2nd century BC' (Winnett's chronology). Coordinates from Wikidata Q1021610.

name: Nashshan
why: Wikipedia 'Nashshan': 'originally independent ... later subsumed into the territory of the ancient Kingdom of Ma'in between the 6th and 4th centuries BC'; allied with Saba in the 8th century BC.

name: Yathill
why: Wikipedia 'Baraqish' (ancient Yathill/Athrula): 'origins are very archaic, possibly 1000 BCE, but it reached its peak ... when it became the capital of the Minaean Kingdom'; 'people lived in the town up to the 1960s, but it has since been abandoned, and is at present occupied by the military'.

name: Qarnaw
why: Wikipedia 'Qarnawu': 'presumably founded at the time the Minaean Kingdom appeared in about 500 BCE ... became the capital of Ma'in for a time'; 'at the end of the Minaean Kingdom in the 1st century BCE, Qarnawu lost its importance, and was probably abandoned not long after'.

name: Zabid
why: Wikipedia 'Zabid': 'the town was the capital of several ruling dynasties in Yemen over many centuries', starting with the Ziyadids (founded early 9th century, 'up to 1016'); a UNESCO World Heritage town that still exists, though 'placed on the List of World Heritage in Danger'.

name: Taiz
why: Wikipedia 'Taiz': 'the first reference to Taiz in historical sources dates back to the first half of the 12th century CE'; made capital of Yemen in 1175 and again later; a major modern Yemeni city (population c. 940,600) not yet shown in the atlas.

name: Sohar
why: Wikipedia 'Sohar': 'an ancient capital of the country that once served as an important Islamic port town on the Gulf of Oman'; 'by the 10th century, Sohar was one of the richest ports of the Persian Gulf'. Founding date before the 10th-century peak is a general-knowledge estimate (approx). Continues today as a major Omani city.

name: Julfar
why: Wikipedia 'Julfar': 'Julfar's rise, efflorescence and fall took place between 1300 and 1650 CE'; predecessor settlement to, but distinct from, the modern city of Ras Al Khaimah.

name: Qal'at al-Bahrain
why: Wikipedia 'Qal'at al-Bahrain': capital of the Dilmun civilisation; 'occupants from 2300 BC up to the 18th century'; 'the place prospered till 1800 BC after which it was deserted' (before later reoccupations).

name: Ikaros
why: Wikipedia 'Failaka Island': 'Failaka was settled following 2000 BC'; known to the Greeks as 'Ikaros'; 'traces of human settlement can be found on Failaka dating back to as early as the end of the 3rd millennium BC, and extending until the 20th century AD'. The island retains a small population today.

name: Thaj
why: Wikipedia 'Thaj': 'the city of Thaj generally dates back to the 3rd century BCE, during the Hellenistic period'; 'by the 13th century, Yaqut referred to it as a spring and village'. Now an uninhabited archaeological site.

name: Timna (Qataban)
why: Wikipedia 'Qataban': 'an ancient Yemenite kingdom in South Arabia that existed from the early 1st millennium BCE to the late 1st or 2nd centuries CE', 'centred around the Wadi Bayhan, and its capital was the city of Timna''. No dedicated Wikipedia article gives coordinates for the Timna' ruins; position is a general-knowledge estimate near Wadi Bayhan (approx), flagged accordingly.

name: Koumbi Saleh
why: Wikipedia 'Koumbi Saleh': 'may have been the capital of the Ghana Empire'; 'radiocarbon dating suggests that the site was occupied between the late 5th and 14th centuries, with the urban period extending approximately from the 11th to the 14th centuries'.

name: Awdaghust
why: Wikipedia 'Aoudaghost': 'the earliest layers date from the 7-9th centuries'; became part of the Ghana Empire c. late 10th/early 11th century; 'the town appears to have been partly abandoned at the end of the 12th century and was completely abandoned by the 15th, although there was some resettlement two centuries later'.

name: Tadmekka
why: Wikipedia 'Essouk': 'the ruins of the medieval town of Tadmakka lie 2 km northeast of the present village'; 'between the 9th and the 15th centuries Tadmekka served as an important entrepot for the trans-Saharan trade'.

name: Niani
why: Wikipedia 'Niani, Guinea': 'the village became the capital in the early 12th century'; 'some scholars believe ... Niani remained continuously the capital through the 14th to 16th centuries'; described by Ibn Khaldun and Leo Africanus. The modern village of Niani still exists on the site.

name: Gao-Saney
why: Wikipedia 'Gao-Saney': 'occupied by roughly 700CE, and was a center of manufacturing, iron smelting, and trade'; 'at some point no later than the early 10th century the Songhay king moved to the site of Gao Ancien ... a few kilometers from Gao Saney', after which Gao-Saney declined.

name: Kukiya
why: Wikipedia 'Kukiya, Mali': 'an early capital of the Songhai people, preceding the founding of the city of Gao'; 'Kukiya was for generations the seat of the Sunni dynasty before they captured Gao in the mid 15th century'.

name: Djenné-Djeno
why: Wikipedia 'Djenné': 'excavations ... indicate that Djenne-Jeno was first settled around 200 BC'; 'after 1100 AD the population of Djenne-Djeno declined and by 1400 AD the site had been abandoned', while the nearby town of Djenne itself continued. Djenne-Djeno has no separate Wikipedia article (it redirects to Djenne), so no qid is given here (Djenne's own qid would otherwise be misattributed).

name: Njimi
why: Wikipedia 'Njimi': 'the capital of the Kanem-Bornu Empire until the 14th century'; 'perhaps established as early as the 8th century'; captured by the Bilala in the 14th century; 'still a prominent location until at least the 16th century, though its old medieval buildings had been abandoned by that point'; exact site never relocated archaeologically, so coordinates are a general-knowledge estimate near the Kanem heartland east of Lake Chad (approx).

name: Ngazargamu
why: Wikipedia 'Ngazargamu': 'the capital of the Kanem-Bornu Empire from the city's foundation in the 15th century to its destruction and abandonment in the Fula jihads in the early 19th century'.

name: Timbuktu
why: Wikipedia 'Timbuktu': 'began as a seasonal settlement and became permanent early in the 12th century'; continues today as a Malian city, not yet shown in the atlas.

name: Djenné
why: Wikipedia 'Djenné': 'preliminary archaeological excavations at sites within modern Djenné indicate that the present town was first settled after 1000 AD'; continues today, distinct from the earlier mound of Djenné-Djeno nearby.

name: Oualata
why: Wikipedia 'Oualata': 'at the beginning of the thirteenth century Oualata replaced Aoudaghost as the principal southern terminus of the trans-Saharan trade'; continues today as a World Heritage oasis town.

name: Ouadane
why: Wikipedia 'Ouadane': first written reference is Portuguese, 'middle of the 15th century', but the trade route it served is described from the 11th century onwards; continues today as a partly-ruined UNESCO town.

name: Chinguetti
why: Wikipedia 'Chinguetti': 'the city was founded in AD 777'; 'by the 11th century, Chinguetti had become a trading center'; continues today, famous for its ancient libraries.

name: Tichit
why: Wikipedia 'Tichit': 'the town of Tichitt was founded in the 12th century as a caravan stop on the Trans-Saharan trade route'; still populated in the early 20th century though 'desertification and sand encroachment have led to the abandonment of many structures' (approx continuation).

name: Azougui
why: Wikipedia 'Azougui': 'in the eleventh century it was the first capital of the Almoravid dynasty'; a village of the same name continues at the site in Mauritania today.

name: Takedda
why: Wikipedia 'Takedda': 'in the 14th century (possibly also earlier and later) the Tuareg-controlled kingdom of Takedda ... played a prominent role in long-distance trade, notably owing to the importance of its copper mines'. Precise founding/decline dates not given by Wikipedia (approx, general knowledge).

name: Bilma
why: Wikipedia 'Bilma': 'the poet Abu Ishaq Ibrahim al-Kanemi was born in Bilma in the 12th century', implying an established town by then; continues today as a Niger oasis town.

name: Agadez
why: Wikipedia 'Sultanate of Agadez': 'the seat of the Sultanate [was transferred] to the then recently (1413) founded Agadez'; continues today as a major city in Niger.

name: Begho
why: Wikipedia 'Begho': 'Begho was founded in the 11th century'; 'oral traditions state that Begho was destroyed by the Ashanti Empire in the mid-18th century, triggering the dispersal of its population', though it 'persisted in a reduced form into the early 19th century'.

name: Bono Manso
why: Wikipedia 'Bono Manso': 'Founded c. 1000 CE, it was the capital of the Bono state from the 11th century to 1723'.

name: Elmina
why: Wikipedia 'Elmina': 'the first European settlement in West Africa'; Portuguese gold trade recorded from 1487; continues today as a Ghanaian town of about 33,576 people.

name: Larabanga
why: Wikipedia 'Larabanga': 'known for its whitewashed adobe Sahelian mosque ... said to date from 1421 ... having been built at the height of the trans-Saharan trade'; continues today.

name: Loropéni
why: Wikipedia 'Loropéni': 'the medieval stone ruins of Loropeni ... date back at least a thousand years'; a market town continues at the site today.

name: Ife
why: Wikipedia 'Ife' (Ile-Ife): 'an ancient Yoruba city ... founded sometime between the years 1000 BC and 500 BC'; 'by 900 AD, the city had become an important West African emporium'. Continues today as a major Nigerian city, not yet shown in the atlas.

name: Old Oyo
why: Wikipedia 'Old Oyo': ruined capital of the Oyo Empire; pavements dated to the '13th and 14th centuries'; 'the site of a ruined medieval city ... has been abandoned since 1835'.

name: Igbo-Ukwu
why: Wikipedia 'Igbo-Ukwu': 'researchers ... commonly describe ancient Igbo-Ukwu as flourishing between approximately the ninth and twelfth centuries'; a specialised, far-reaching bronze-working society. The modern town of Igbo-Ukwu, Anambra State, continues at the site.

name: Nri
why: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Nri': 'a king list reconstructed from oral genealogies places the beginning of the dynasty around the tenth century'; ritual/political influence contracted from the late 17th century. The town of Nri, Anambra State, continues today.

name: Great Zimbabwe
why: Wikipedia 'Great Zimbabwe': 'settled from around 1000 AD, and served as the capital of the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe from the 13th century'; 'the city was abandoned in the 16th or 17th century'.

name: Mapungubwe
why: Wikipedia 'Kingdom of Mapungubwe': the capital moved from Schroda (c. 900) to Bambandyanalo/K2 (c. 1000) to Mapungubwe Hill ('around 1220'); 'its growth has been linked to the decline of Mapungubwe from around 1300'.

name: Khami
why: Wikipedia 'Khami': 'the capital of the Torwa dynasty for about 200 years from around 1450'.

name: Danangombe
why: Wikipedia 'Naletale': 'the Torwa dynasty founded Khami in the 15th century and Dhlo Dhlo in the 16th century'. End date approximated to the collapse of Rozvi power in the 1830s under Ndebele pressure (general knowledge).

name: Naletale
why: Wikipedia 'Naletale': the Torwa dynasty 'relocat[ed] their capital to Nalatale in the 17th century'; occupied 'through the eighteenth to nineteenth centuries during Rozvi rule'. End date approximated to the collapse of Rozvi power in the 1830s (general knowledge).

name: Thulamela
why: Wikipedia 'Thulamela': 'a kingdom was formed at Thulamela in the 13th century'; 'Butua's collapse in the 17th century into civil war likely led to Thulamela's isolation ... and its abandonment soon after'.

name: Manyikeni
why: Wikipedia 'Manyikeni': 'occupation of the site begins at about 1200 AD and lasting until 1700 AD'.

name: Ingombe Ilede
why: Wikipedia 'Ingombe Ilede': recent dating shows 'occupations involving major social differentiation and long-distance trade ... are not earlier than the late 15th century', with glass-bead trade continuing into the 17th century.

name: Chibuene
why: Wikipedia 'Chibuene': 'the current estimate for the development of the site is estimated to be around 400 AD'; 'the archaeological site was occupied from approximately AD 600 to AD 1700 continuously and into the present, intermittently'.

name: Bigo bya Mugenyi
why: Wikipedia 'Bigo bya Mugenyi': 'the Bigo earthworks have been dated to roughly AD 1300-1500'; described as Uganda's 'largest and most important ancient monument'. Coordinates are a general-knowledge estimate for the Katonga River earthworks in Sembabule District (approx).

name: Ntusi
why: Wikipedia 'Ntusi': 'a Late Iron Age archaeological site ... that dates from the tenth century to the fifteenth century AD'; 'radiocarbon dates from Ntusi are from 1000 to 1400 AD'. Coordinates are a general-knowledge estimate for Ntusi, Sembabule District, Uganda (approx).

name: Engaruka
why: Wikipedia 'Engaruka': 'sometime in the 15th century, an Iron Age farming community built a large continuous village area'; 'Engaruka was abandoned at latest in the mid-18th century'.

name: Kibiro
why: Wikipedia 'Kibiro' gives excavation methodology but few explicit settlement dates; the salt-working village on Lake Albert is generally understood (general knowledge, approx) to have been occupied since around the 14th century and continues today.

name: Kilwa Kisiwani
why: Wikipedia 'Kilwa Kisiwani': 'recent excavations and Carbon-14 dating of the site have confirmed its founding at the start of the 9th century CE'; centre of the Kilwa Sultanate at its height in the 13th-15th centuries; 'still home to a small and resilient community' today.

name: Songo Mnara
why: Wikipedia 'Songo Mnara': 'the stone town was occupied from the 14th to 16th centuries'.

name: Gedi
why: Wikipedia 'Gede, Kenya': 'extensive ruins of a former port have been dated to the thirteenth century or earlier, including a tomb with a date corresponding to 1399, until at least the seventeenth century'. Abandonment date is a general-knowledge estimate (approx).

name: Shanga
why: Wikipedia 'Shanga, Pate Island': 'first inhabited by the Swahili in the eighth century'; 'the Swahili community in Shanga continued to thrive there for 600 years until their disappearance in the early fifteenth century'; 'oral traditions claim that the site was deserted circa 1400-1425'. No coordinates given by the API; position estimated from Pate Island (approx).

name: Pate
why: Wikipedia 'Pate Island': 'according to the Pate Chronicle, the town of Pate was founded by refugees from Oman in the 8th century'; centre of the Pate Sultanate from the 13th century; the town continues today, much diminished.

name: Manda
why: Wikipedia 'Manda Island': the 'prosperous 9th century' port town of Manda 'owes its origins to trade with the Persian Gulf during the 9th and 10th centuries'; 'both Manda town and Takwa were probably abandoned due to a lack of water in the first half of the 19th century'.

name: Mnarani
why: Wikipedia 'Mnarani ruins': 'the settlement at the site dates back to the 14th century'; 'people left this settlement in the early 17th century, supposedly due to a lack of fresh water and raids by neighbors'.

name: Jumba la Mtwana
why: Wikipedia 'Jumba la Mtwana': 'dates back to the fourteenth century'; 'the absence of later sherds suggests that this settlement was abandoned at the beginning of the fifteenth century'.

name: Malindi
why: Wikipedia 'Malindi': 'the city of Malindi, founded around 850 AD ... appears to have been destroyed around 1000 AD'; recovered and 'has existed as a Swahili settlement since at least the 13th century'; continues today as a major Kenyan town.

name: Lamu
why: Wikipedia 'Lamu': 'the town was founded in the fourteenth century'; continues today as a UNESCO World Heritage town.

name: Kaole
why: Wikipedia 'Kaole': 'Kaole was originally settled in the 8th century as a trading town'; ruins 'dating to a period between the 13th century and the 16th century'.

name: Tumbatu
why: Wikipedia 'Tumbatu': 'larger towns such as Tumbatu developed ... in the early second millennium CE'; 'the late medieval city (13th century) was described in a chronicle known as the Tumbatu Manuscript'; the island retains a village today.

name: Unguja Ukuu
why: Wikipedia 'Unguja Ukuu': an early Swahili trading settlement on Zanzibar Island with artefacts from across the Indian Ocean world. Wikipedia's extract does not give explicit founding/decline years; dates are a general-knowledge estimate (early Swahili site, c. 6th-10th centuries), flagged approx.

name: Domoni
why: Wikipedia 'Domoni': 'according to archaeological finds the town was established in the 12th century'; 'in ancient times, Domoni was the capital of the Nzwani sultans' until the capital moved to Mutsamudu; continues today as the second-largest city on Anjouan.

name: Mutsamudu
why: Wikipedia 'Mutsamudu': 'Mutsamudu was likely founded in 1482'; continues today as the capital of Anjouan, Comoros.

name: Sofala
why: Wikipedia 'Sofala': 'sometime in the 10th century, Sofala emerged as a small trading post and was incorporated into the greater global Indian Ocean trade network'; 'at present known as Nova Sofala'; decline followed the Portuguese-era shift of trade to other ports (general knowledge, approx for the rename date).

name: Barawa
why: Wikipedia 'Barawa': 'the town of Barawa was founded by Aw-Ali from the Tunni'; 'Ibn Sa'id in the thirteenth century described Barawa as one of the three most important cities on the East African coast'; continues today as capital of South West State, Somalia.

name: Faza
why: Wikipedia 'Pate Island': 'Faza town, on the North coast, known by the name of Ampaza by the Portuguese, dates back at least to the 14th century'; 'in the 18th century Faza again fell into decline due to the rise of Pate'. Coordinates estimated near Pate Island (approx, general knowledge).

name: Qanbalu
why: Wikipedia 'Ras Mkumbuu': 'Ras Mkumbuu was an important site in Pemba's history, being the site [of] one of the island's most important early settlements, Qanbalu, which is now a ruin'. Qanbalu is mentioned by medieval Arab geographers such as al-Mas'udi (10th century); precise founding/abandonment dates are a general-knowledge estimate (approx).

name: Chwaka
why: Wikipedia 'Chwaka, Pemba': 'the site is believed to be occupied from the 11th century to the 16th century CE'; a medieval Swahili historic site on Pemba Island featuring 'grand mosques' and a harbour.

name: Kizimkazi
why: Wikipedia 'Kizimkazi': 'was once a walled city', now a fishing village on Zanzibar; the nearby Kizimkazi Mosque carries a Kufic inscription conventionally dated 1107 CE (general knowledge, approx), the oldest dated Islamic inscription in East Africa.

name: Dahlak Kebir
why: Wikipedia 'Dahlak Kebir': 'known for its ancient cisterns and necropolis, dating from at least AD 912'; seat of the medieval Dahlak Sultanate in the Red Sea; the village continues today with a population of about 2,500.

name: Khaybar
why: Wikipedia 'Khaybar': Bronze Age settlement at al-Natah in the oasis 'from around 2400 to 1500 BCE'; pre-Islamic Jewish oasis 'conquered by the Muslims under Prophet Muhammad during the Battle of Khaybar in 628 CE'; the oasis town continues today in Medina Province, Saudi Arabia.

name: Fadak
why: Wikipedia 'Fadak': 'a village with fertile land in an ancient oasis ... ninety miles north of Medina'; 'the takeover of Fadak by Muslims in 629 CE was peaceful'. Founding date not given by Wikipedia; approximated as a long-established pre-Islamic oasis village (general knowledge).

name: Daura
why: Wikipedia 'Daura': 'the spiritual home of the Hausa people', one of the Hausa Bakwai states; legend places its founding (Bayajidda) 'in about the 9th century'; continues today as a city in Katsina State, Nigeria.

name: Katsina
why: Wikipedia 'Katsina (city)': 'Katsina is believed to have been founded circa 1100'; 'from the 17th to the 18th century, Katsina was the commercial heart of Hausaland and became the largest of the seven Hausa city-states'; continues today as a major Nigerian city.

name: Berenice Epideires
why: Wikipedia 'Berenice Epideires': 'a town on the western shore of the Red Sea ... located near the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, in modern-day Djibouti', mentioned by Strabo, Pliny and Ptolemy. No explicit founding/abandonment dates are given by Wikipedia; a Ptolemaic-to-Roman-era span is a general-knowledge estimate (approx), flagged accordingly.

name: Debeira
why: Wikipedia 'Debeira': 'the site was occupied by a small town or large village in the middle ages'; 'inhabited between the 7th and 9th centuries, and abandoned after a decline that continued into the tenth century', with later 11th-century redevelopment noted but not detailed further.

name: Hagar Yahirr
why: Wikipedia 'Awsan': 'the name of the capital of Awsan is unknown, but it is assumed to be the tell that is today known as Hagar Yahirr ... the largest settlement in the wadi'; the kingdom's first period 'began in the 8th century BC' and ended when 'Saba, under Karib'il Watar, obliterated Awsan' in the late 7th century BC (a later resurgence is not reflected here). Identification of the capital and its coordinates (Wadi Markha, Yemen) are uncertain and approximate, flagged accordingly.

name: Ocelis
why: Wikipedia 'Ocelis': 'a port on the Red Sea, on the Arabian side near or at Bab al-Mandeb'; the Periplus (1st century CE) describes it as a 'harbour, watering station' on the Egypt-India route. Wikipedia gives no clear abandonment date; end approximated to the general decline of Red Sea emporia after the early Roman period (general knowledge).

name: Al-Balid
why: Wikipedia 'Al-Baleed Archaeological Park': ruins of 'the medieval city of Zafar/Zufar ... acted as an important port for frankincense trade after the decline of the nearby port in Khor Rori'; visited by Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta and Zheng He; 'the city declined in the 16th-17th centuries'. Distinct from the Himyarite Zafar in the Yemeni highlands.

name: Qana
why: Wikipedia 'Bir Ali': 'in pre-Islamic times, the port was called Qani' (Qane, Cana)'; the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (50 CE) describes Cana as 'a market town ... of the frankincense country'. Bir Ali continues today as a village in Shabwah Governorate, Yemen.

name: Muza
why: Wikipedia 'Muza (emporion)': 'an important emporion on the Arabian coast of the Red Sea ... mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, Pliny the Elder's Natural History and Ptolemy's Geography'; 'now it is inland from the modern port city of Mokha due to the recession of the coast'. Rename year to Mokha is a general-knowledge estimate (approx).

name: Sesebi
why: Wikipedia 'Sesebi': 'a New Kingdom Egyptian town ... a temple was built there by Akhenaten, who appointed a viceroy to maintain the structure, govern the local settlement, and secure traffic on the Nile'. Wikipedia gives no abandonment date; end approximated to the close of the New Kingdom (general knowledge).

name: Merca
why: Wikipedia 'Merca': 'mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek travel document dating from the first century AD, as one of a series of commercial ports on the Somali littoral'; considered by Ibn Sa'id (1214-74) 'to be the capital of the Hawiye'; continues today as a Somali city.

name: Tikal
why: Wikipedia 'Tikal': monumental architecture dates back as far as the 4th century BC; the site's abandonment came by the end of the 10th century after a gradual population decline.

name: Calakmul
why: Wikipedia 'Calakmul': seat of the 'Kingdom of the Snake' through most of the Classic period; elite presence continued to AD 900 and stelae were erected into the early 10th century before final abandonment.

name: Palenque
why: Wikipedia 'Palenque': ruins date from ca. 226 BC to ca. AD 799; the city-state 'perished in the 8th century' with no new elite construction after 800.

name: Copán
why: Wikipedia 'Copán': first stone architecture built about the 9th century BC; the city's collapse 'occurred sometime between 800 and 830 AD'.

name: Caracol
why: Wikipedia 'Caracol': the epicentral area was occupied 'no earlier than 650 BC and lasted no later than AD 950'; Structure A6 was abandoned in AD 1050, 'the final abandonment of the site'.

name: El Mirador
why: Wikipedia 'El Mirador': flourished from about the 6th century BC; after a brief Late Classic reoccupation the area was 'again nearly completely abandoned' by about AD 900.

name: Uxmal
why: General knowledge: Uxmal rose as a Puuc-style capital around the 7th century AD and was largely abandoned by the Terminal Classic/early Postclassic, c. AD 1000 (approximate).

name: Mayapan
why: Wikipedia 'Mayapan': 'the political and cultural capital of the Maya ... during the Late Post-Classic period from the 1220s until the 1440s'; the site 'was abandoned sometime in the 15th century'.

name: Tulum
why: Wikipedia 'Tulum': achieved its greatest prominence between the 13th and 15th centuries; occupied about 70 years after Spanish exploration began, 'abandoned by the end of the 16th century'.

name: Yaxchilan
why: Wikipedia 'Yaxchilan': a long-running dynasty from at least the early 5th century; king K'inich Tatb'u Skull III's 808 victory 'probably represented the final overthrow ... ending dynastic rule there and destroying the city as a capital'.

name: Bonampak
why: Wikipedia 'Bonampak': its structures date to the Late Classic (c. AD 580-800); 'Bonampak collapsed with Yaxchilan in the 9th century'.

name: Piedras Negras
why: Wikipedia 'Piedras Negras (Maya site)': already 'a city of some importance since 400 AD'; 'the site was abandoned by AD 930'.

name: Dos Pilas
why: Wikipedia 'Dos Pilas': founded in AD 629; a small refugee village was 'overrun and itself abandoned in the early years of the 9th century AD, at which point the history of Dos Pilas as a settlement ends'.

name: Aguateca
why: Wikipedia 'Aguateca': occupied 'from about 200 B.C. until about 800 A.D., when the city was attacked and ransacked'; 'completely abandoned around 830 AD'.

name: Naranjo
why: Wikipedia 'Naranjo (Maya site)': occupied 'from about 500 BC to 950 AD, with its height in the Late Classic Period'; final abandonment linked to political turmoil and drought dated to 810 AD.

name: Yaxha
why: Wikipedia 'Yaxha': first settlement founded in the Middle Preclassic (c. 1000-350 BC); eclipsed by Naranjo in the Late Classic (AD 600-900), consistent with the general Maya collapse (approximate).

name: Seibal
why: Wikipedia 'Seibal': first settled around 900 BC; refounded in AD 830 but 'by 930 AD, the site was completely abandoned'.

name: Cancuén
why: Wikipedia 'Cancuén': a major Classic-period trade centre peaking in the 7th century; a massacre of the ruling family 'occurred around 800 AD' after which the city was 'abandoned ... and subsequently not re-occupied' (founding date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Toniná
why: Wikipedia 'Toniná': an 8th-century text refers to a king ruling in AD 217; the site has 'the last known Long Count date on any Maya monument, marking the end of the Classic Maya period in AD 909'.

name: Quiriguá
why: Wikipedia 'Quiriguá': occupied 'as early as the Late Preclassic (400 BC - AD 200)'; 'in the 9th century there was a severe decline in population, culminating in the abandonment of the city'.

name: Kaminaljuyu
why: Wikipedia 'Kaminaljuyu': 'primarily occupied from 1500 BC to 1200 AD'; now largely destroyed beneath modern Guatemala City.

name: Iximche
why: Wikipedia 'Iximche': 'the capital of the Late Postclassic Kaqchikel Maya kingdom from 1470 until its abandonment in 1524'.

name: Q'umarkaj
why: Wikipedia 'Qʼumarkaj': founded by king Qʼuqʼumatz 'around 1400'; captured and burned by Pedro de Alvarado's Spanish forces in 1524.

name: Zaculeu
why: Wikipedia 'Zaculeu': first occupied in the Early Classic (AD 250-600), capital of the Postclassic Mam kingdom; 'in AD 1525 the city was attacked by Spanish conquistadors' and its last ruler surrendered.

name: Mixco Viejo (Jilotepeque Viejo)
why: Wikipedia 'Mixco Viejo': the Chajoma king Lajuj No'j moved his capital here from Ochal 'around 1450'; 'in 1525 Pedro de Alvarado sent a small company to conquer' the Poqomam capital of the same name.

name: Takalik Abaj
why: Wikipedia 'Takalik Abaj': earliest occupation towards the end of the Early Preclassic, c. 1000 BC; the Kʼicheʼ conquest around AD 1000 meant 'the original inhabitants abandoned the city they had occupied for almost two millennia'.

name: Chinkultic
why: Wikipedia 'Chinkultic': flourished in the Maya Classic era 'from about the 3rd through the 9th century'; 'Post-Classic-Era occupation ... continued until the 13th century, after which it was abandoned'.

name: Comalcalco
why: General knowledge: Comalcalco, the westernmost known Maya city, flourished in the Classic period (c. AD 250-900), building uniquely in fired brick for lack of local limestone (dates approximate).

name: Champotón
why: Wikipedia 'Champotón, Campeche': known anciently as Chakanputun, 'a city of the Maya civilization dating back to at least the 10th century'; conquered by Spain and refounded as 'Villa de San Pedro Champotón' in 1538.

name: Chunchucmil
why: Wikipedia 'Chunchucmil': most populous in the Middle Classic (AD 400-650); Terminal Classic occupation 'is ephemeral at best' with squatter-like Postclassic settlement (dates approximate).

name: San Gervasio
why: Wikipedia 'San Gervasio (Maya site)': 'founded around 300 CE'; 'by about 1200, San Gervasio had become the largest settlement on Cozumel and remained so until the arrival of the Spanish in the early 16th century' (coordinates approximate).

name: Oxkintok
why: Wikipedia 'Oxkintok': chronology 'starts at ~600 BCE and lasts until ~1500 CE', fading out completely towards 1500 CE with no evidence of occupation after it was abandoned.

name: Edzna
why: Wikipedia 'Edzna': 'may have been inhabited by as early as 600 BC'; 'Edzná was already inhabited by 400 BC, and was abandoned c. 1500 AD'.

name: Kabah
why: Wikipedia 'Kabah (Maya site)': 'inhabited from the mid-3rd century BCE'; latest carved date 987 CE, most architecture built 7th-11th centuries CE.

name: Sayil
why: Wikipedia 'Sayil': 'first was settled circa AD 800'; the city 'was abandoned by c. AD 1000, a pattern of rapid growth and decline ... typical of the Puuc region'.

name: Labná
why: Wikipedia 'Labna': 'the city existed from 200 to 1000 AD', reaching its peak from 800 to 1000 AD.

name: Xpuhil
why: Wikipedia 'Xpuhil': 'the INAH estimates occupation to be somewhere between 300 and 1200 AD'.

name: Dzibilchaltun
why: Wikipedia 'Dzibilchaltun': 'continuously occupied for thousands of years', expanding and contracting between a mid-sized city and small town before Spanish contact (dates approximate).

name: Izamal
why: Wikipedia 'Izamal': 'founded during the Late Formative Period (750-200 BC) and was continuously occupied until the Spanish Conquest'; a Spanish colonial city was founded atop it in the 16th century, and the modern town of Izamal continues today.

name: Coba
why: Wikipedia 'Coba': 'first settled between 50 BC and 100 AD'; remained important into the Post-Classic, with new temples built 'until at least the 14th century, possibly as late as the arrival of the Spanish'; the adjacent modern village of Coba continues today.

name: Ek Balam
why: Wikipedia 'Ekʼ Balam': became capital of a Maya kingdom 'around the beginning of the Common Era'; population 'decreased dramatically ... during the Postclassic period as Ekʼ Balam was slowly becoming vacant' (dates approximate).

name: Uaxactun
why: Wikipedia 'Uaxactun': dated inscriptions run to the 8th Baktun (AD 328); no erection of dedicatory monuments recorded after AD 711, though ceramic occupation continued into the Postclassic (end date approximate).

name: Motul de San José
why: Wikipedia 'Motul de San José': 'first settled between 600 and 300 BC'; continuous occupation 'until the Early Postclassic, up to around AD 1250'.

name: Holmul
why: Wikipedia 'Holmul': 'began its existence around 800 BCE and was abandoned by 900 CE at around the time of the Classic Maya collapse'.

name: Nakbe
why: Wikipedia 'Nakbe': habitation began 'during the Early Formative period (c. 1400 BC)' and continued 'until its collapse during the Terminal Formative period (100-200 CE)'.

name: El Zotz
why: Wikipedia 'El Zotz': significant expansion in the 6th century AD; jointly engaged in battle against Tikal with Naranjo in the 8th century AD, after which the site declines (end date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Río Azul
why: Wikipedia 'Río Azul': earliest major architecture 'around 500 BC'; 'largely abandoned in the 6th century' with a Late Classic resurgence, consistent with the general Maya collapse by c. AD 830 (end date approximate/general knowledge).

name: La Corona
why: Wikipedia 'La Corona': the Classic-period Maya court residence known ancienly as Sak-Nikte', identified as long-sought 'Site Q'; occupation span approximate/general knowledge for the Classic period.

name: Holtun
why: Wikipedia 'Holtun': 'had a long period of occupation that lasted from the Middle Preclassic through to the Late Classic periods' (end date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Uxbenka
why: Wikipedia 'Uxbenka': 'the earliest-known Maya polity in the southern Belizean lowlands', with occupation dated to the Early Classic (ca. 250-500 CE) and continuing into the Late Classic (end date approximate).

name: Nim Li Punit
why: Wikipedia 'Nim Li Punit': flourished 'from the 5th century AD through the 8th century AD'; occupation 'ceased rather suddenly in the 9th century AD'.

name: Lubaantun
why: Wikipedia 'Lubaantun': 'flourishing from the AD 730s to the 890s, and seems to have been completely abandoned soon after'.

name: Pusilha
why: Wikipedia 'Pusilhá': the kingdom was 'founded shortly before the beginning of the Late Classic period' (c.570); occupation continued 'through to the post-classic' with a decline thereafter (end date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Cahal Pech
why: Wikipedia 'Cahal Pech': habitation dated 'as far back as 1200 BCE'; 'the site was abandoned in the 9th century CE for unknown reasons'.

name: Xunantunich
why: Wikipedia 'Xunantunich': grew significantly from AD 600-670; left in abandonment c. AD 750 before a partial revival in the Tsak' phase (AD 780-890), after which the site declines (end date approximate).

name: Altun Ha
why: Wikipedia 'Altun Ha': occupied 'for many centuries, from about 900 B.C.'; 'gradual abandonment of the site began in 800' and 'by the beginning of the eleventh century, the site of Altun Ha was completely abandoned' (a limited reoccupation followed to the 15th century).

name: Lamanai
why: Wikipedia 'Lamanai': 'occupied as early as the 16th century BC'; unlike most southern lowland sites it 'was not abandoned at the end of the 10th century AD', continuing to be occupied 'up to the 17th century AD'.

name: San Andrés
why: Wikipedia 'San Andrés (El Salvador)': occupation began 'around the year 900 BC'; last evidence of pre-Hispanic activity dates 900-1200 AD, with decline linked to the El Boquerón eruption of AD 964-1040.

name: Tazumal
why: Wikipedia 'Tazumal'/'Chalchuapa': occupied from the Classic period through the Postclassic; after 1200 'occupation shift[ed] westwards towards the centre of what is now the modern town of Chalchuapa', which 'was still occupied at the time of the Spanish conquest'.

name: Nixtun-Ch'ich'
why: Wikipedia 'Nixtun-Chʼichʼ': major grid-planned construction occurred before AD 200 in the Middle-Late Preclassic; 'the site was also occupied in the Late Classic through the Colonial period (AD 600-1734)'.

name: Nojpetén
why: Wikipedia 'Nojpetén': also known as Tayasal, 'founded when the Itza fled south around 1441-1446'; 'fell to a Spanish assault in 1697; it was the capital of the last Maya kingdom to fall to the conquerors'. The island is now occupied by the modern town of Flores.

name: San Bartolo
why: Wikipedia 'San Bartolo (Maya site)': earliest identifiably Maya inscriptions found here date to the 3rd century BC; the pyramid was 'constructed from ca 300 BC ... and completed ca 50 AD' (end date approximate).

name: Monte Albán
why: Wikipedia 'Monte Albán': 'founded toward the end of the Middle Formative period at around 500 BC'; 'the ancient capital was largely abandoned' by AD 900-1000.

name: Mitla
why: Wikipedia 'Mitla': 'perhaps from as early as 900 BCE'; 'still occupied and functioning as the main religious center when the Spanish ... arrived' in the 1520s; the modern town of Mitla continues on the site today.

name: Yagul
why: Wikipedia 'Yagul': first occupied around 500-100 BC, functioning as the capital of a Postclassic city-state until 'occupied at the time of the Spanish Conquest', after which the population relocated to modern Tlacolula.

name: Zaachila
why: Wikipedia 'Zaachila': became 'the final Zapotec capital after Monte Albán fell'; 'founded in 1399' by one theory; 'the Mixtecs took control of the capital prior to the arrival of the Spaniards'. Modern Zaachila continues on the site.

name: Guiengola
why: Wikipedia 'Guiengola': a Late Postclassic (14th-early 16th century) fortified Zapotec city near Tehuantepec, besieged by Mexica armies according to 16th-century sources (end date approximate/general knowledge for the Spanish conquest period).

name: Coixtlahuaca
why: Wikipedia 'Coixtlahuaca': defeated by the Mexica under Moctezuma I in the 15th century and became a tributary province capital; a modern village of the same name continues on the site (founding date and coordinates approximate/general knowledge).

name: Yanhuitlán
why: Wikipedia 'Santo Domingo Yanhuitlán': the pre-Hispanic Mixtec city-state of Yanhuitlán (Yodzocahi) was conquered by Tizoc and rebelled again in 1506; a Dominican-founded town continues on the site (founding date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Tututepec
why: Wikipedia 'Tututepec': founded by the Mixtec ruler Eight Deer, whose 'migration led ... to the coast' is dated to the late 11th century; became capital of a tributary empire until the Spanish conquest. The modern town of Villa de Tututepec de Melchor Ocampo continues on the site.

name: El Tajín
why: Wikipedia 'El Tajín': the settlement was 'founded in the 1st century CE'; it 'prospered until the early years of the 13th century, when it was destroyed by fire, presumably started by an invading force believed to be the Chichimecs'.

name: Xochicalco
why: Wikipedia 'Xochicalco': 'founded in about 650 AD by the Olmeca-Xicallanca'; 'at some point around 900 CE the city ... was burned and destroyed'.

name: La Venta
why: Wikipedia 'La Venta': the Olmec occupation at La Venta 'dates to 1200 BCE'; 'after 500 years of pre-eminence, La Venta was all but abandoned by the beginning of the fourth century BCE'.

name: San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán
why: Wikipedia 'San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán': 'the major center of Olmec culture from 1400 BCE to 900 BCE'; 'was the largest city in Mesoamerica from roughly 1200 BCE until 900 BCE'.

name: Tres Zapotes
why: Wikipedia 'Tres Zapotes': 'founded some time in the centuries before 1000 BCE'; 'may have been abandoned by 900 CE, although there was a smaller and later occupation'.

name: Izapa
why: Wikipedia 'Izapa': 'may have been settled as early as 1500 BCE'; 'remained occupied through the Early Postclassic period, until approximately 1200 CE'.

name: Cempoala
why: Wikipedia 'Cempoala': 'founded at least 1,500 years before the arrival of the Spanish'; defeated by the Aztecs in the mid-15th century then allied with Cortés against them in the 16th century. A modern town continues on the site.

name: Cantona
why: Wikipedia 'Cantona (archaeological site)': prominent 'between 600 and 1000 CE'; 'it was abandoned after AD 1050' following Chichimec invasions.

name: Cacaxtla
why: Wikipedia 'Cacaxtla': capital of the Olmeca-Xicallanca, prospering 650-900 CE; 'its ascendancy came to an end around 900 CE and, by 1000, the city had been abandoned'.

name: Chiapa de Corzo (Zoque site)
why: Wikipedia 'Chiapa de Corzo (Mesoamerican site)': 'rose to prominence around 700-500 BCE'; significant changes/decline occurred during the Istmo phase (300-400 CE).

name: Azcapotzalco
why: Wikipedia 'Azcapotzalco (altepetl)': capital of the Tepanec empire; 'founded in the 13th century' (other sources say 995 AD); the Tepanec empire fell in 1428 when Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan conquered it. Modern Azcapotzalco continues on the site (coordinates approximate).

name: Culhuacan
why: Wikipedia 'Colhuacan (altepetl)': traditionally 'the first Toltec city'; 'survived the fall of Tollan and maintained its prestige until the mid-14th century'. Modern Culhuacán continues on the site (coordinates approximate).

name: Xochimilco
why: Wikipedia 'Xochimilco (altepetl)': 'the city of Xochimilco was founded in 919'; 'in 1430, the Mexica of Tenochtitlan succeeded in conquering the city'. Modern Xochimilco continues on the site (coordinates approximate).

name: Chalco
why: General knowledge: the Chalco confederacy of altepetl was conquered by Tenochtitlan under Axayacatl in the mid-1460s; the modern town of Chalco continues on the site (founding date and end date approximate).

name: Tlacopan
why: Wikipedia 'Tlacopan': a Tepanec city-state, originally subordinate to Azcapotzalco, that in 1428 joined Tenochtitlan and Texcoco as the third member of the Aztec Triple Alliance. The neighbourhood of Tacuba, Mexico City, continues on the site (coordinates approximate).

name: Tlatelolco
why: Wikipedia 'Tlatelolco (altepetl)': founded in 1337 by dissident Mexica; after the Spanish conquest of 1521 the Spanish 'established the ruins of Mexico-Tenochtitlan as the Spanish capital of New Spain', absorbing Tlatelolco.

name: Tetzcoco
why: Wikipedia 'Tetzcoco (altepetl)': 'Xolotl was said to be the founder of Tetzcoco in 1115 AD'; one of the largest and most prestigious cities of central Mexico until the Spanish occupied it in 1520-21. Modern Texcoco de Mora continues on the site.

name: Coatlinchan
why: Wikipedia 'Coatlinchan': the Acolhua 'established Coatlinchán as their capital until around 1337, when the capital was moved to Tetzcoco'. The modern town of San Miguel Coatlinchán continues on the site (founding date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Huexotla
why: Wikipedia 'Huejotla': one of the most important Acolhua cities alongside Tetzcoco and Coatlinchan, its 'development began in the 13th century' (end date and coordinates approximate/general knowledge).

name: Tenayuca
why: Wikipedia 'Tenayuca': 'considered to be the earliest capital city of the Chichimec', traditionally founded ca. 1224; 'by the mid-14th century the power of Tenayuca had already waned, it was conquered and replaced as a regional power by nearby Azcapotzalco'.

name: Malinalco
why: Wikipedia 'Malinalco': dominated by the Matlazinca before Aztec conquest in the 1470s, when a sanctuary for Eagle and Jaguar warriors was built; the modern town of Malinalco continues on the site (founding date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Quiahuiztlan (Tlaxcala)
why: Wikipedia 'Quiahuiztlan': one of the four altepetl of the Tlaxcala confederation, absorbed into the modern city of Tlaxcala (dates approximate/general knowledge).

name: Tizatlan
why: Wikipedia 'Tizatlan': one of the four altepetl of the Tlaxcallan confederation, 'the third ... to be founded'; ruled by Xicotencatl the Elder at the time of the Spanish conquest (dates approximate/general knowledge).

name: Tula
why: Wikipedia 'Tula de Allende': the Toltecs 'rose to power after 713 CE'; 'usually identified as the Toltec capital around 980 CE, the city was destroyed at some time between 1168 and 1179'. Modern Tula de Allende continues on the site.

name: Caral
why: Wikipedia 'Caral': 'Caral was inhabited from around 2600 BC to 2000 BC', the largest recorded site of its age in the Andean region.

name: Sechín Bajo
why: Wikipedia 'Sechin Bajo': a circular plaza there was 'constructed in 3500 BCE', among the oldest civic centres in the Americas (clamped to -3400); ruins date from 3500 BCE to 1300 BCE.

name: Cerro Sechín
why: Wikipedia 'Cerro Sechín': 'dating to 1600 BC', believed by Julio C. Tello to be the capital of the Casma/Sechin culture (end date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Chavín de Huántar
why: Wikipedia 'Chavín de Huántar': ruins 'constructed as early as 1200 BC, and occupied until around 400-500 BC by the Chavín'; its primary religious function 'had ceased prior to 400 BC'.

name: Tiwanaku
why: Wikipedia 'Tiwanaku': 'a statistical assessment of reliable radiocarbon dates estimates that the site was founded around AD 110'; 'the society appeared to have collapsed around AD 1000'.

name: Wari
why: Wikipedia 'Wari (archaeological site)': 'founded ca. 400 AD and gained prominence around 550 AD'; 'the city was abandoned ca. 1000 AD'.

name: Pikillaqta
why: Wikipedia 'Pikillaqta': 'the site was occupied from about 550 to 1100 AD and around 1100 AD is when it was ultimately abandoned'.

name: Viracochapampa
why: General knowledge: Viracochapampa, a Wari administrative centre near Huamachuco, was occupied during the Middle Horizon (dates approximate, as Wikipedia gives only relative chronological phases).

name: Marcahuamachuco
why: Wikipedia 'Marcahuamachuco': construction 'began around AD 400 ... and continued until approximately 800 AD'; 'the site was likely abandoned in the 15th century' after Inca conquest in the 14th century.

name: Cerro Baúl
why: Wikipedia 'Cerro Baúl': a Wari political outpost and ceremonial centre of the Middle Horizon (AD 400-1000); occupied contemporaneously with Tiwanaku influence (dates approximate/general knowledge; coordinates approximate).

name: Chan Chan
why: Wikipedia 'Chan Chan': 'believed to have been constructed around 850 AD by the Chimú'; capital of Chimor 'from 900 to 1470, when they were defeated and incorporated into the Inca Empire'.

name: Túcume
why: Wikipedia 'Túcume': constructed as 'the new Late Sican capital'; a major regional centre through the Lambayeque/Sican (800-1350), Chimú (1350-1450) and Inca (1450-1532) occupations. A modern town of the same name continues on the site.

name: Pachacamac
why: Wikipedia 'Pachacamac': adobe construction dated to the Lima culture (3rd-7th centuries AD); the oracle city functioned until 'shortly before the arrival and conquest by the Inca Empire' and on into the Spanish conquest era (end date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Cerro Blanco (Moche capital)
why: Wikipedia 'Huaca del Sol'/'Huaca de la Luna': the twin huacas 'are major components of the ancient Moche capital city of Cerro Blanco'; Huaca del Sol was built in the Moche civilisation period (AD 100-800) and Huaca de la Luna 'was inhabited between the 1st and 9th century AD'.

name: El Brujo
why: General knowledge: the El Brujo archaeological complex in the Chicama Valley was occupied from Cupisnique through Moche times, with its Moche-period heyday to around AD 700 (dates approximate, as the article gives little explicit chronology).

name: Pacatnamú
why: Wikipedia 'Pacatnamu': occupied through a Moche then a Chimu period; 'the date usually given for the end of the main period of occupation of Pacatnamu is around A.D. 1370', linked to the Chimú conquest of the Jequetepeque valley.

name: Paramonga
why: Wikipedia 'Paramonga': 'an important city constructed at the border of the former Kingdom of Chimor ... during the late Intermediate Period (AD 1200 to 1400)'.

name: Vilcashuamán
why: General knowledge: Vilcashuamán was built as a major Inca administrative and ceremonial centre in the mid-15th century; its role ended with the Spanish conquest, and a modern town of the same name continues on the site (dates approximate/general knowledge).

name: Huánuco Pampa
why: Wikipedia 'Huánuco Pampa': one of the Inca 'New Cuscos'; briefly occupied by Spanish conquerors who founded a city there in 1539 before quickly relocating it to Pillco (founding date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Choquequirao
why: Wikipedia 'Choquequirao': a 15th- and 16th-century Inca settlement, possibly founded by Pachacuti; 'after its abandonment in the late 16th century, Choquequirao was reclaimed by the dense Andean forest'.

name: Ollantaytambo
why: Wikipedia 'Ollantaytambo': 'around the mid-15th century, the Inca emperor Pachacuti conquered and razed a pre-existing town of Ollantaytambo' and rebuilt it as his royal estate; the town 'has some of the oldest continuously occupied dwellings in South America' and continues under the same name today.

name: Vilcabamba (Espíritu Pampa)
why: Wikipedia 'Vilcabamba, Peru': 'the capital of the Neo-Inca State from 1539 to 1572', when 'a Spanish army ... made a final advance on the Incas' remote jungle capital'.

name: Cusco
why: Wikipedia 'Cusco': 'the city was originally founded in the 12th century by Manco Cápac, as the capital of the Kingdom of Cusco and, later, of the Inca Empire'; it continues today as a modern Peruvian city of the same name. Note: Cusco appears to be missing from the atlas's general city list entirely (it is not a Pleiades-adjacent 'ancient town' case so much as an apparent gap in the main city dataset) -- flagged for the user's attention.

name: Chucuito
why: Wikipedia 'Chucuito': 'important in pre-Inca times ... described by Pedro De Cieza De Leon', held to be the oldest site in the region and a major centre of power of the Lupaca kingdom before Inca conquest c.1450; the modern small town of Chucuito continues on the site (dates approximate/general knowledge).

name: Kuélap
why: Wikipedia 'Kuélap': built by the Chachapoya culture, with human occupation from the 5th century AD and most structures built 900-1100 AD; occupied 'during the final centuries before the Spanish conquest' (end date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Cahuachi
why: Wikipedia 'Cahuachi': 'a major ceremonial center of the Nazca culture, based from about 1-500 CE'; 'abandoned around 450-500 CE, due to a severe drought and after severe mudslides and earthquakes'.

name: Moundville
why: Wikipedia 'Moundville Archaeological Site': 'the site was occupied by Native Americans of the Mississippian culture from around 1000 AD to 1450 AD'; abandoned by the mid-16th century when Hernando de Soto's army passed through the region.

name: Etowah
why: Wikipedia 'Etowah Indian Mounds': 'built and occupied in three phases, from 1000-1550 CE', occupied by 'a series of cycling chiefdoms' of the Mississippian culture.

name: Spiro
why: Wikipedia 'Spiro Mounds': a major Mississippian settlement 'from 800 to 1450 AD'; 'the mound area was abandoned about 1450, but nearby communities persisted until 1600 CE'.

name: Paquimé
why: Wikipedia 'Casas Grandes' (also known as Paquimé): 'settlement began after 1130 AD'; 'the community was abandoned approximately in 1450 AD'.

name: Angel Mounds
why: Wikipedia 'Angel Mounds': 'the large residential and agricultural community was constructed and inhabited from AD 1100 to AD 1450, and served as the political, cultural, and economic center of the Angel chiefdom'.

name: Kincaid Mounds
why: Wikipedia 'Kincaid Mounds': the Mississippian culture occupation 'developed from the local Lewis community about 1050 CE'; 'Mississippian culture occupation at the site appears to have ended by 1400-1450 CE'.

name: Town Creek
why: Wikipedia 'Town Creek Indian Mound': built by the Pee Dee people 'as early as 980 CE'; 'an important ceremonial site occupied from about 1150-1400 CE'.

name: Ocmulgee
why: Wikipedia 'Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park': major earthworks 'built before 1000 CE' with a Late Mississippian (Lamar) period continuing to 1350-1600 CE.

name: Emerald Mound
why: Wikipedia 'Emerald Mound Site': 'constructed during 1250 and 1600 CE', the type site for the Emerald Phase (1500-1680) of the Natchez Bluffs Plaquemine culture, used as a ceremonial centre for outlying villages.

name: Winterville
why: Wikipedia 'Winterville site': 'this civilization thrived from about 1000 to 1450 CE'; 'by AD 1450 the Winterville Mound site appears to have been abandoned completely'.

name: Grand Village of the Natchez
why: Wikipedia 'Grand Village of the Natchez': construction 'began ... about 1200 CE'; occupied by the historic Natchez people until conflict with the French in the early 18th century (end date approximate/general knowledge).

name: Nodena
why: Wikipedia 'Nodena site': 'around 1400-1650 CE an aboriginal palisaded village existed in the Nodena area'; abandoned before Quapaw occupation by the 1670s.

name: Parkin (Casqui)
why: Wikipedia 'Parkin Archeological State Park': 'around 1350-1650 CE an aboriginal palisaded village existed at the site'; 'continuously occupied for at least 500 years' before Quapaw occupation by the 1670s.

name: Cofitachequi
why: Wikipedia 'Cofitachequi': a Mississippian paramount chiefdom in the Wateree valley whose capital shifted between Belmont Neck, Talimeco/Adamson and Mulberry (Camden, South Carolina); occupation from the 10th century, mainly after 1200, into the 17th century (coordinates approximate/general knowledge, being the Camden, SC area).

name: Coosa
why: Wikipedia 'Coosa (town)': the capital of the Coosa paramount chiefdom encountered by Hernando de Soto, with 'a large plaza and three platform mounds'; 'by the close of the 16th century, most of the core area of the Coosa was abandoned' (coordinates approximate/general knowledge).

name: Hawikuh
why: Wikipedia 'Hawikuh Ruins': 'founded around 1400 AD'; the Zuni pueblo encountered by Coronado in 1540, destroyed during the Pueblo Revolt period in 1680 (end date general knowledge).

name: Pecos Pueblo
why: Wikipedia 'Pecos National Historical Park': 'the first Pecos pueblo was one of two dozen rock-and-mud villages built in the valley around AD 1100'; the pueblo was finally abandoned in 1838 (general knowledge for the final abandonment date; coordinates for the pueblo itself, not the wider park).

name: Snaketown
why: Wikipedia 'Hohokam Pima National Monument': Snaketown 'is dated by some scholars to around 300 BCE'; 'it is not particularly clear what caused the abandonment of Snaketown around 1100 CE'.

name: Hochelaga
why: Wikipedia 'Hochelaga (village)': a 16th-century St Lawrence Iroquoian fortified village on or near Mount Royal, linked to 'the occupation of the area by the St. Lawrence Valley [Iroquoians] between 1200 and 1600 CE'; the site is now within Montreal, founded nearby in 1642.

name: Stadacona
why: Wikipedia 'Stadacona': 'a 16th-century St Lawrence Iroquoian village not far from where Quebec City was founded in 1608'; Samuel de Champlain 'chose the location of the village' for his colony (founding date approximate/general knowledge).

name: La Navidad
why: Wikipedia 'La Navidad': a fort 'Christopher Columbus and his crew built ... in 1492'; 'the first European settlement established in the New World during the Age of Discovery', destroyed by indigenous people the following year.

name: La Isabela
why: Wikipedia 'La Isabela': 'the first stable Spanish settlement and town in the Americas', established late 1493/early 1494 by Columbus; 'La Isabela was abandoned by 1500'.

name: Kuhikugu
why: General knowledge: Kuhikugu, at the headwaters of the Xingu River, was the largest of some twenty Xinguano towns and villages mapped by Michael Heckenberger; this Xinguano urban complex is generally dated to roughly AD 1250-1650, ending amid post-contact collapse (dates approximate/general knowledge, as the Wikipedia extract does not itself give a date range).

name: Luoyang
why: Wangcheng was built beside Chengzhou in the Zhou era and became the primary Eastern Zhou capital 771-510 BC; the Han dynasty built Luoyang over the same ground in 25 AD, and it remained a leading imperial capital (Wei, Jin, Northern Wei, Tang 'Eastern Capital', Song 'Western Capital') until the Northern Song era, after which it declined to a secondary city. Exact correspondence between the Wangcheng and Chengzhou sites is unclear in the source articles, so dates are approximate.

name: Daliang
why: King Hui of Wei relocated his capital to the newly built city of Daliang in 361 BC. Renamed Bianliang/Dongjing, it became 'the largest city in the world from 1013 to 1127' as Northern Song capital, before falling to the Jin in 1127; it kept administrative importance afterward and reverted to the name Kaifeng under the Ming in 1368.

name: Yin
why: 'At the beginning of the 14th century BC, King Pangeng of the Shang dynasty established his capital... The city, known as Yin, was the first stable capital in Chinese history', serving 12 kings until the Shang fell to the Zhou in 1046 BC. The site continued as a county seat (as Zhangde from later dynasties) and was renamed Anyang in 1912.

name: Xianyang
why: Minister Shang Yang 'organized the relocation of Qin's administration' to the newly built city of Xianyang in 350 BC, which became the capital of the unified Qin empire in 221 BC; Xiang Yu 'killed Ziying and burned Xianyang' in 206 BC. The present-day city, re-founded nearby in 1371, is a distinct but continuing settlement next to Xi'an.

name: Ye
why: 'Ye was first built in the Spring and Autumn period by Duke Huan of Qi' (reigned 685-643 BC, so the founding date is estimated); it later served as capital of Later Zhao, Ran Wei, Former Yan, Eastern Wei and Northern Qi. In 580 the city 'was razed to the ground' by forces of the future Sui founder and its people relocated to Anyang, so it did not continue.

name: Ying
why: Ying, near modern Jingzhou, became capital of the State of Chu; Wikipedia gives several competing dates for the move (706-689 BC) but 'traditional sources' have King Wen establishing it in 689 BC. It remained capital (with a brief interruption after a Wu sack in 506 BC) until a Qin army under Bai Qi forced the court to flee to Chen in 278 BC. Coordinates are an estimate for the Jinancheng ruin site, as Wikipedia gives none.

name: Shouchun
why: 'Shou, formerly known as Shouchun... was the last capital of the State of Chu from 241 BCE', after the court fled the sack of Chen, until Chu fell to Qin around 223 BC. The town continued afterwards as a county seat, eventually named Shou County; exact founding and renaming dates are estimated.

name: Kuaiji
why: Around the time of Yue's King Goujian (early 5th century BC) 'his people began establishing permanent centers in the alluvial plain', with a fortification built by his advisor Fan Li in what is now Shaoxing's Yuecheng district; the settlement was known as Kuaiji until renamed Shaoxing in 1131 during the Song dynasty. The city, with a population over five million, remains prosperous today.

name: Xintian
why: 'In 585 BCE, the Jin State moved their capital to Xintian, an ancient city located in present-day Houma... Xintian remained the capital until the fall of the Jin State in 376 BCE.' A famous bronze-casting site was found there. The modern name and city status date to the 20th century (approximate).

name: Yong
why: 'The city of Yong... was once the capital of the ancient State of Qin' (founded 677 BC per the Yong disambiguation page) until the capital moved to Yueyang in 383 BC. The town continued as Yong County and was renamed Fengxiang under the Tang dynasty, when it also briefly served as a secondary imperial 'Western Capital'.

name: Xiadu
why: 'The Xiadu or Lower Capital of Yan... may have been the largest city in the world from 400 to 300 BC, with an estimated peak population over 300,000', with excavated palaces, cemeteries and large bronze- and iron-casting workshops. Wikipedia gives no explicit destruction date; the end date used is the fall of the state of Yan to Qin in 222 BC, drawn from general historical knowledge rather than the article itself.

name: Pingcheng
why: The Han dynasty 'founded a site within present-day Datong in 200 BC' called Pingcheng, which 'became the capital of the Xianbei-founded Northern Wei dynasty from AD 398-494' before Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital to Luoyang. The city was renamed Datong in 1048 and later served as a Liao/Jin secondary 'Western Capital' and Ming garrison town; it remains a significant coal city today.

name: Xiangping
why: Liaoyang is 'one of the oldest continuously-inhabited cities in northeast China, dating back to before the Warring States period', when it was Xiangping, capital of Liaodong Commandery. It served as the Jin dynasty's eastern capital Dongjing and, from 1621, as Nurhaci's Later Jin capital (also named Dongjing) until the Manchus moved their capital to Shenyang in 1625, after which it reverted to a regional city named Liaoyang.

name: Shangjing
why: Founded in 918 by Liao emperor Yelu Abaoji as his imperial capital and formally named Shangjing Linhuangfu in 938, modelled on Tang Chang'an with a Khitan 'Imperial City' and a Han Chinese 'Han City'. Jurchen Jin forces sacked it in 1120 and it lost capital status by 1150; it 'was destroyed by the Mongol armies in 1214 and left abandoned afterwards'.

name: Zhongjing
why: The Liao dynasty's 'Central Capital' Zhongjing Dading Fu was established around 1009 on the Five Capitals System; the Jurchen Jin dynasty later conquered and reused it, first as their own Middle Capital and then, after moving their court to Beijing, as a Northern Capital. There is no dedicated Wikipedia article; this relies on brief mentions in the Ningcheng County and Five Capitals System articles plus general knowledge of the Jin dynasty's fall in 1234, so dates and location (near Daming Town, about 20km from the county seat) are approximate.

name: Huiningfu
why: Huining Fu 'served as the first superior capital of the Jurchen-led Jin dynasty (1115-1234) from 1122 to 1153', built on a Chinese-style plan by the architect Lu Yanlun. The capital moved to Yanjing (Beijing) in 1153, and 'in 1157, Wanyan Liang even went so far as to destroy all palaces in his former capital', though it briefly resumed secondary-capital status after 1173.

name: Kaiping
why: Shangdu, 'originally named Kaiping, was established between 1252 and 1256' by Liu Bingzhong for Kublai Khan and renamed Shangdu in 1264 as the Yuan summer capital (the 'Xanadu' of Marco Polo and Coleridge). 'In 1369, during the fall of the Yuan dynasty, Shangdu was sacked by Ming forces and largely destroyed', and the site was never resettled.

name: Shangjing Longquanfu
why: 'Shangjing Longquanfu was established as the permanent capital' of the Balhae (Bohai) kingdom in 756 near Lake Jingpo, and served as capital (with an interruption from 785-793) 'from 756 to 785, and again from 793 to 926', modelled on Tang Chang'an at about a fifth of its size. The kingdom, and the city's role, ended with the Liao conquest of Balhae in 926.

name: Erlitou
why: 'A settlement emerged around 1860 BCE, and later became the largest settlement in the Yiluo Basin', reaching about 24,000 people and 300 hectares with palaces, bronze-casting workshops and China's earliest known road network; it is a leading candidate for a capital of the Xia dynasty, or possibly an early Shang capital (Bo). 'After the end of the Erligang culture [c. 1300 BC], the settlement was abandoned'; radiocarbon estimates for the culture's span vary (1900-1500 or 1750-1530 BC), so dates are approximate.

name: Sizhou
why: Sizhou 'existed intermittently from 580 to 1912' as a prefectural or subprefectural seat on the Si River; under the Qing, 'the subprefectural seat at Sizhou was entirely submerged within Hongze Lake in 1680, along with the nearby Ming Zuling tombs', after which government moved to Xuyi and Si County. Wikipedia gives no coordinates for the submerged town, so its position on the historic Hongze Lake shore near Xuyi County is an estimate from general geography.

name: Xiangyang
why: Xiangyang County was established at this strategic site on the Han River in the early Western Han dynasty and kept the name for over 2,000 years. It was the capital of Jing Province under the warlord Liu Biao, and under the Southern Song became a garrison city that, with Fancheng, withstood a six-year Mongol siege (the Siege of Xiangyang) before surrendering. Merged with Fancheng in 1950 as Xiangfan, renamed back to Xiangyang in 2010.

name: Tainan
why: Established by the Dutch East India Company in 1624 as Fort Zeelandia; Taiwan's oldest city and, for 263 years, its capital under Dutch rule, the Kingdom of Tungning and Qing dynasty rule, until the provincial capital moved to Taichung and then Taipei in 1887. Continues today as a special municipality and a global semiconductor manufacturing hub.

name: Danyang
why: The first capital of the State of Chu, enfeoffed to Xiong Yi by King Cheng of Zhou (r. 1042-1021 BC) at the junction of the Dan and Xi Rivers near present-day Xichuan County, Henan; Wikipedia's Xichuan County article confirms 'the state of Chu's first capital Danyang was in Xichuan.' Chu's capital moved south-east to Ying sometime between 695 and 689 BC after 'more than 400 years' at Danyang. Location is approximate, per the Chu (state) article and the hint.

name: Jinyang
why: No standalone Wikipedia article exists; its history is covered within the Taiyuan article. The first ancient city of Jinyang was built in 497 BC around the southern Jinyuan district of present-day Taiyuan by Dong Anyu, steward of the Jin official Zhao Jianzi. It served as capital or secondary capital of Zhao, the Qin commandery of Taiyuan, Former Qin, and later Northern Han, among others. In 979 the Song Emperor Taizong, after a long siege, flooded and burned the city following the Northern Han surrender; it was 'completely abandoned' and a new city (modern Taiyuan, already covered elsewhere in the atlas) was founded in 982 on a different site. Distinct site from the modern city; coordinates are for Jinyuan District, approximate.

name: Shangqiu
why: Traditionally the base of the Predynastic Shang, with the Shang dynasty's first capital Nanbo just to its south; after the Zhou conquest c. the 11th century BC the area became the state of Song, whose capital Suiyang stood here. Suiyang later served as the Han-era capital of the Liang Kingdom, and, briefly in 1127, as a Southern Capital of the fleeing Northern Song court. The current name Shangqiu 'appeared in 1545'; the city continues today as a prefecture-level city.

name: Qufu
why: The state of Lu 'made Qufu their capital throughout the Spring and Autumn period', after the Duke of Zhou's son Bo Qin was enfeoffed there following the Zhou conquest (c. 1042 BC); Lu was conquered by Chu in 249 BC. Qufu is the birthplace of Confucius and home to the Temple, Cemetery and Mansion of Confucius (San Kong), a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994; it continues today as a county-level city and a living centre of Confucian pilgrimage.

name: Anyi
why: No standalone 'Anyi' article exists; Wikipedia's Wei (state) article records that Wei's capital 'was moved from Anyi to Daliang (present-day Kaifeng) during the reign of King Hui' (usually dated 361 BC), after which Wei was also called Liang. Wikipedia's Xia County article, covering the same district, states it 'served as the previous capitals of the Xia dynasty and the Wei kingdom'. Dates for the founding (after the 453 BC partition of Jin) and the move are approximate, drawing partly on general historical knowledge.

name: Pingyao
why: 'There was already a settlement in place at Pingyao by the reign of the Xuan King' of Zhou (c. 827-782 BC), when earthen ramparts were raised; it belonged to Jin and then Zhao during the Warring States period, and was known as Pingtao under the Qin. Its surviving walls date from 1370 (Ming). By the 16th century it was a regional financial hub and by the late 19th century the financial centre of the Qing Empire, a status that collapsed with the 1911 Xinhai Revolution (its leading bank, Rishengchang, went bankrupt in 1914). Continues today as a UNESCO World Heritage town (1997), 'the only walled city seat in China to survive with both its historic street plan and its original building fabric substantially intact'.

name: Dali
why: The old town, formerly known as Xiemie, 'was the medieval capital of both the Bai kingdom Nanzhao (779-902) and the Kingdom of Dali (937-1253)'. It 'was razed and its records burnt during its conquest by China's Yuan Dynasty'; the present old town was organised in the late 14th century under the Hongwu Emperor. Continues today as a major Yunnan tourist destination.

name: Guangling
why: The Wu hegemon Fuchai built the Han (Hangou) Canal linking the Yangtze to the Huai by 486 BC and 'established a fortress to protect the southern end' the following year; the area was later organised as Guangling Commandery under the Han. The Sui renamed the city Yangzhou in 590 AD, though the name Guangling was later restored under the Tang; Yangzhou briefly served as the Southern Song's capital in 1128-1129. Continues today as a prefecture-level city on the Grand Canal.

name: Jingdezhen
why: 'The town was established during the Jin dynasty under the name Changnan', renamed Fuliang in 742 CE and Jingdezhen in 1004, after the era name of Emperor Zhenzong of Song, whose reign saw its porcelain first rise to fame; it began making porcelain even earlier, under the Han. Known as the 'Porcelain Capital', producing Chinese ceramics for at least 1,000 years; it kept the character zhen ('town') in its name even after becoming a prefecture-level city in 1953, and its kiln sites were UNESCO-listed in 2026.

name: Tongwancheng
why: Built in 419 by about 100,000 Xiongnu under Helian Bobo as the capital of the Xiongnu-led Hu Xia dynasty, on the edge of the Ordos Desert; its name means 'the city ruling ten thousand'. Due to worsening desertification, in 994 'Emperor Taizong ordered the destruction of the city and the relocation of its residents'; it 'gradually fell into ruin and was completely abandoned by the early Ming dynasty', before being rediscovered in 1845.

name: Fenghuang
why: Wikipedia's Fenghuang County article states the ancient town 'was built in 1704, and has 300 years of history', under the name Zhen'gan; it was renamed Fenghuang after 1913. It contains the Southern China Great Wall, a Ming-dynasty fortification against Miao attacks, and was the centre of the Miao Rebellion of 1854-73. Continues today as a well-preserved Ming/Qing-style walled tourist town; note Wikipedia's 1704 construction date is later than the Tang/Ming framing in the candidate hint.

name: Weishan
wikipedia: Weishan Yi and Hui Autonomous County
