why: The old town, described by Wikipedia's Gongchen Tower article as 'the old town and seat of Weishan ... of Nanzhao', is traditionally the early seat of Mengshe, the polity from which the Nanzhao kingdom grew; local Yi people 'claim direct descent from Xinuluo, the founder of Mengshe (Nanzhao)'. Its Ming-era (1390) city wall and Gongchen Tower, a symbol of the town until a 2015 fire, stood over the town 'then called Menghua'; the name Weishan replaced Menghua in the 1950s. Continues today as the seat of Weishan Yi and Hui Autonomous County. The founding date rests partly on general historical knowledge of Nanzhao's origins rather than a direct Wikipedia statement.

name: Liaocheng
why: During the Spring and Autumn period the area 'was part of the State of Qi as Liaocheng Town'; the Grand Canal later flowed through it. Its prefecture was renamed Dongchang Circuit in 1276 and became Dongchang Prefecture under the Ming, a name that lasted until the prefecture-level city of Liaocheng was created in 1998 and the old county-level core became Dongchangfu District. Continues today as a prefecture-level city on the Grand Canal.

name: Xinzheng
why: Duke Wu of Zheng 're-established the state of Zheng in modern-day Xinzheng (meaning New Zheng)' in support of King Ping of Zhou, around 770 BC; after Han conquered Zheng it became the capital of the state of Han, until 'Han was the first [of the seven Warring States] to fall, in 230 BC', with a failed restoration rebellion at 'former capital Xinzheng' in 226 BC. Continues today as a county-level city under Zhengzhou.

name: Lingshou
why: Wikipedia's Zhongshan (state) article states the capital city Lingshou 'is believed to have been founded in 380, and to have remained the capital until 296, when Zhongshan was conquered' (by Zhao). Its ruins, with palace foundations, workshops and cemeteries, were found in 1976 in Sanji, Pingshan County, Hebei -- per Wikipedia's King Cuo of Zhongshan article, 'near the ancient city of Lingshou' -- not in the modern, separately-located Lingshou County named in the candidate hint. Coordinates use Pingshan County and are approximate.

name: Loulan
why: Wikipedia describes Loulan (native name Kroraina/Kroran) as "an important oasis city along the Silk Road", "already known as far back as the 2nd century BCE" and the fortified capital of the Tarim Basin kingdom later renamed Shanshan; the Chinese envoy Zhang Qian described it as a fortified city near Lop Nur in 126 BCE. It "was abandoned in 330 CE, probably owing to lack of water when the Tarim River... changed course", with the garrison moved south.

name: Niya
why: Wikipedia's Niya ruins article describes the site (Han-era Chinese name Jingjue, native name Cad́ota) as "a major commercial center on an oasis" on the southern Silk Road, with the Hanshu recording it as an independent oasis state with its own king's seat, commandant and officials. "Niya became part of Loulan Kingdom by the third century" and "towards the end of the fourth century it was under Chinese suzerainty. Later it was conquered by Tibet." The site's abandonment date around the 4th-5th century CE (commonly attributed to desiccation) is not given explicitly in the extract, so this is a general-knowledge estimate; coordinates are likewise approximate general knowledge as the Wikipedia infobox carries none.

name: Jiaohe
why: Wikipedia states "From 108 BC to 450 AD Jiaohe was the capital of the Anterior Jushi Kingdom", a fortified natural-cliff city with a Tang-era population of 7,000, "an important stop along the Silk Road trade route". It continued as a prefecture seat under Jin, Tang and the Uyghur Khaganate until "it was finally abandoned after its destruction during an invasion by the Mongols led by Genghis Khan in the 13th century"; the exact year is not given, so 1220 is an approximate mid-campaign estimate.

name: Gaochang
why: Wikipedia says Gaochang (also Khocho, Qocho, Karakhoja) "was built in the 1st century BC" as "a busy trading center" and "stopping point for merchant traders travelling on the Silk Road", later the capital of the Gaochang Kingdom and then the Uyghur Kingdom of Qocho/Karakhoja. "It was destroyed in wars during the 14th century", giving only a century-level end date.

name: Khara-Khoto
why: Wikipedia states "Built in 1032, the city thrived under the rule of the Tangut-led Western Xia dynasty" and continued to flourish and expand under Mongol/Yuan rule; it is identified with Marco Polo's Etzina. Ming annals record its capture in 1372, but a Hermitage curator's analysis of the finds concludes "it seems that the life of the town ceased sometime around 1380", after which "the city was abandoned and left in ruins."

name: Turpan
why: Wikipedia notes "the historical centre of the prefectural area has shifted a number of times, from Yar-Khoto (Jiaohe)... to Qocho (Gaochang)... and to Turpan itself", with the name Turfan/Turpan only becoming widespread in the post-Mongol/2nd-millennium period, after Gaochang's 14th-century destruction. Turpan remains a prefecture-level city and major oasis and fruit-growing centre today (population 693,988, 2020); no precise founding year is given, so 1400 is an approximate estimate for when Turpan itself became the region's centre.

name: Kucha
why: Wikipedia describes Kucha as "an ancient Tocharian Buddhist kingdom" and "the most populous oasis in the Tarim Basin", controlled by the Xiongnu by the 2nd century BCE and recorded in the Book of Han as the largest of the Thirty-six Kingdoms with a population over 81,000. Its Buddhist-era capital and Subashi Temple were "abandoned in the 13th century" as the ancient kingdom declined, though the site continues today as the modern town of Kuqa, seat of Kuqa County; the founding date before Han-era records is a general-knowledge estimate.

name: Hotan
why: Wikipedia describes the ancient Kingdom of Khotan as "one of the earliest Buddhist states in the world", with Sampul-area cemeteries dated 300 BCE to 100 CE showing settlement in the region well before then. It remained an independent Buddhist city-state (some 400 temples by the early 10th century) until "the Karakhanid leader Yusuf Qadir Khan conquered Khotan around 1006", ending "local autonomy of this southern Tarim city state"; Hotan continues today as a county-level city (population 408,900, 2018) and the last Xinjiang municipality with a majority Uyghur core population.

name: Hami
why: Wikipedia states Hami's oldest endonym Cumuḍa dates to when it "was founded by a people known in Han Chinese sources as the Xiao Yuezhi..., during the 1st millennium BCE", and it has been "known for its production of agricultural products and raw resources" since the Han dynasty. Hami (also Kumul) continues today as a prefecture-level city known for Hami melons, with no clear end to its ongoing significance.

name: Dunhuang
why: Wikipedia states "Dunhuang Commandery was probably established shortly after 104 BC" as one of four Han frontier garrison towns, becoming a key Silk Road entrepôt and site of the Mogao Caves; by the 2nd century CE it "had a population of more than 76,000". Its Silk-Road-era prominence waned when "the Silk Road was officially abandoned during the Ming dynasty" and the city "went into a steep decline", though it was later resettled under the Qing (1725) and survives today as a county-level city and major heritage tourism centre.

name: Zhangye
why: Wikipedia states "Zhangye Commandery was established by Western Han in 111 BC", making it a key Hexi Corridor frontier outpost and later, under its alternative name Ganzhou, capital of the Western Xia and a stop recorded in Marco Polo's Travels. It remains a prefecture-level city today (population over 1.1 million). The exact years the name alternated between Zhangye and Ganzhou are not given, so those transition points are approximate.

name: Wuwei
why: Wikipedia states "people began settling here about 5,000 years ago" and that, as ancient Guzang or Liangzhou, the city "found importance as the capital of various states at the eastern terminus of the Hexi Corridor" and "became an important provincial capital during the Former Han dynasty"; Zhangye's own article notes its Han commandery seat was originally "at the site of modern Wuwei", founded 111 BC, supporting that date here. Wuwei remains a prefecture-level city today (population 1,464,955, 2020).

name: Jiuquan
why: Wikipedia states "Fulu was founded in 111 BC as an outpost in the Hexi Corridor near the Yumen Pass along the overland Silk Road", later renamed Suzhou under the Sui and Jiuquan Commandery under the Tang; it was "the great center of the rhubarb trade" and remains a prefecture-level city today, home to the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center. The precise year of the modern renaming from Suzhou to Jiuquan is not stated in the extract, so 1913 (commonly cited to distinguish it from Suzhou, Jiangsu) is a general-knowledge estimate.

name: Karasahr
why: Wikipedia describes Karasahr (Chinese exonym Yanqi, native Agni/Ārśi) as "an ancient town on the Silk Road", a "relatively large and important" Han-era kingdom already established when Chinese sources first describe it. "By the mid-9th century, the area had been conquered by the Uyghur Khaganate" and "Agnideśa became widely known by the Uyghur Turkic name Karasahr". The town continues today as capital of Yanqi Hui Autonomous County (population 31,773 in 2006).

name: Aksu
why: Wikipedia records Aksu as the kingdom of Gumo from at least the Former Han dynasty (125 BCE), "described as a 'kingdom' containing 3,500 households and 24,500 individuals", later known in the Buddhist era as Baluka/Bharuka when Xuanzang visited in 629 CE. "In 1207-1208, Aksu submitted to Genghis Khan", ending its run as a contested independent city-state; it continues today as a county-level city and seat of Aksu Prefecture.

name: Almaliq
why: Wikipedia describes Almaliq as "a medieval city in the Ili basin", "originally one of Karluk cities in the Turkic Kaganates", which became a major Islamic centre under Tughluq Temur (c. 1351-1363) and hosted Nestorian Christian and Catholic communities (Franciscan missionaries recorded there in 1339). No founding year is given in the extract, so 900 CE is a general-knowledge estimate for its Karluk-era origin; its eventual abandonment (commonly attributed to Timur's late-14th-century campaigns) is likewise a general-knowledge estimate, not stated in the article.

name: Beshbalik
why: Wikipedia states Beiting/Ting Prefecture was established there after "the pacification of Gāochang in the fourteenth year of the zhēnguān era (640)"; the Old Turkic name Beshbalik ("five cities") first appears in a 713 inscription, and the city became a capital of the Uyghur Khaganate and then the Kingdom of Qocho. "Due to military struggles between the Chagatai Khanate and the Yuan dynasty..., the city was abandoned and lost its prosperity in the late 13th century."

name: Afrasiyab
why: Wikipedia: Afrasiyab 'is an ancient site in northern Samarkand...that was occupied from c. 500 BC to 1220 AD prior to the Mongol invasion', with habitation beginning in the 7th-6th century BC as a Sogdian centre. It is 'the oldest part and the ruined site of the ancient and medieval city of Samarkand', on a hilly mound north of the modern city. Coin finds show occupation into the 13th century, ending with Genghis Khan's sack; the population then relocated and the Timurids built a new Samarkand slightly south/west of the Afrasiyab mound, which is why this is kept distinct from the atlas's continuing Samarkand entry.

name: Parab
why: Wikipedia: 'The city has a history dating back to the time of the Achaemenid Empire, when it was known as Parab', later a Turkic dynastic capital called Turarband 'that was later to be called Otrar'. Genghis Khan besieged it for five months in 1219, breaching the walls and massacring the inhabitants in 1220, but it revived as a trade centre under the Mongols and Timur (who died there in 1405). It declined through the 17th-18th centuries as the Silk Road lost importance: 'By the end of the 18th century, there were only 40 families remaining in Otrar, compared to perhaps 5,000-7,000 in the 14th to 17th centuries.'

name: Panjakent
why: Wikipedia: 'Ancient Panjakent was a small but flourishing town of the Sogdians in pre-Islamic Central Asia', known as Panchekanth, which 'grew in the 5th century AD'. 'In AD 722, Arab Muslim forces besieged and took the town'; the last ruler Divashtich was captured and executed, and 'towards the end of the 8th century the town on the upper terraces was depopulated and relocated' - the ruins now lie on the outskirts of the modern city of the same name.

name: Bukhara
why: Wikipedia: 'Dating to pre-Islamic antiquity, Bukhara became a major centre of Islamic sciences and scholarship', a major city of the Samanid Empire and Karakhanid Khanate, 'devastated during the Mongol invasion under Genghis Khan in the 13th century but recovered under the Timurid Empire', then capital of the Uzbek Khanate/Emirate of Bukhara until 'The Emirate of Bukhara was abolished after the Russian Revolution in 1920.' Exact founding date is not given in the extract (general knowledge places the oasis settlement in the mid-1st millennium BC), hence approx.

name: Khiva
why: Wikipedia: 'According to archaeological data, the city was established around 2,500 years ago' (celebrated its 2,500th anniversary in 1997). It became 'the former capital of Khwarezmia, the Khanate of Khiva, and the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic'; the Khanate of Khiva's rule ended with Russian annexation/the establishment of the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic in 1920, taken as the end of its heyday as a khanal capital, though the city continues today.

name: Gurganj
why: Wikipedia: archaeological finds at Kyrkmolla Hill show 'the town already had a strong structure in the 5th and 4th centuries BC'. Gurganj 'rose to prominence between the 10th and 14th centuries as the Khwarezmian capital'; Genghis Khan 'destroyed the city' in 1221 and Timur razed it again in 1388, after which decline continued 'until the 16th century, when it was replaced as a regional capital by Khiva and was ultimately abandoned' - the extract's summary states 'the inhabitants of the ancient city deserted it in the early eighteenth century', after which the site 'has remained undisturbed ever since'.

name: Nisa
why: Wikipedia: Nisa 'was an ancient settlement of the Parthians...described by some as the first seat of the Arsacid Empire', 'traditionally assumed to have been founded by Arsaces I (reigned c. 250 BC-211 BC)' and reputedly a royal residence, later renamed Mithradatkert by Mithridates I (r. c. 171-138 BC). 'Nisa was totally destroyed by an earthquake during the 1st decade BC.'

name: Termez
why: Wikipedia: 'One of Central Asia's oldest towns, Old Termez...was established sometime before the 3rd century BC', later Alexander the Great's Alexandria on the Oxus and a Kushan-era Buddhist centre. It was destroyed by Genghis Khan in 1220 ('all the people...were driven out onto the plain...and slain') but rebuilt nearby; abandoned again in the later 18th century, then revived and renamed Termez (from Pattakesar) in 1928, continuing as a city today.

name: Kesh
why: Wikipedia: 'Historically known as Kesh or Kish, Shahrisabz...It was founded more than 2,700 years ago and formed a part of the Achaemenid Empire...from the 6th to 4th centuries BC.' 'It has been known as Shahrisabz since the Timurid era' - it is 'primarily known today as the birthplace of 14th-century Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur', whose Aq Saray palace there was begun in 1379.

name: Cyropolis
why: Wikipedia: 'Khujand may have been the site of Cyropolis...established when King Cyrus the Great founded the city during his last expedition against the Saka tribe...shortly before his death'; 'After being captured by Alexander the Great in 329 BC, it was renamed Alexandria Eschate'. It dates 'back about 2,500 years to the Persian Empire' and was 'formerly known as Leninabad from 1936 to 1991'.

name: Osh
why: Wikipedia: Osh 'is the oldest city in the country (estimated by UNESCO to be more than 3,000 years old)', with a bazaar 'which has been taking place on the same spot for the past 2,000 years' as a major Silk Road market; Sulayman Mountain there is thought by some to be Ptolemy's 'Stone Tower' marking the midpoint of the Silk Road.

name: Talas
why: Wikipedia: Taraz's '2,000th anniversary (recognized by UNESCO) in 2001' dates 'from a fortress built in the area by a Xiongnu Chanyu named Zhizhi' and 'the Battle of Zhizhi in 36 BCE'; 'first recorded under the name "Talas" in 568 CE', a major Silk Road trade centre and site of the Battle of Talas (751 CE). Renamed Auliye-Ata (1864), Mirzoyan (1936), Dzhambul (1938), and Taraz again in 1993.

name: Isfijab
why: Wikipedia: 'The city celebrated the 3,000th anniversary of its founding in 1999', making it 'one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the World'. 'The oldest name of the city...is Isfijab...which remained until the Mongol conquest'; Kashgari also records it already being called Sayram, the name that stuck afterwards. It is significant today for its surviving mud-brick architecture.

name: Suyab
why: Wikipedia: 'The settlement of Sogdian merchants sprang up along the Silk Road in the 5th or 6th century.' Suyab was 'the principal capital of the Western Turkic Khaganate' under Tong Yabghu Qaghan, then a Tang dynasty military outpost and one of the Four Garrisons of the Anxi Protectorate until 719. 'It is believed to have been supplanted by Balasagun in the early 11th century and was abandoned soon after.'

name: Balasagun
why: Wikipedia: 'Founded by the Kara-Khanid Khanate in the ninth century, Balasagun soon supplanted Suyab as the main political and economical centre of the Chu Valley' and 'was the capital of the Kara-Khanid Khanate from the 10th century until it was taken by the Qara Khitai...in 1134', then 'captured by the Mongols in 1218'. 'Since the 14th century, Balasagun is a village with plenty of ruins', its Nestorian Christian graveyard still in use into that century.

name: Sighnaq
why: Wikipedia: 'in the 10th century there was a semi-sedentary city of the Oghuz Turks'; 'In the twelfth century it was the capital of the khanate of Kipchak'. Genghis Khan 'conquered the region after a siege in 1220' and 'the population was massacred'; it later became capital of the Blue Horde and was fought over by Timurids, Uzbeks and Kazakhs until, 'in the sixteenth century, it belonged to the Kazakhs, but it lost importance and eventually disappeared.'

name: Yasi
why: Wikipedia: Turkistan 'has an archaeological record dating back to the 4th century' and 'prior to Ahmad Yasawi's era...the city was referred to as Iasy (Yasi)'. After Timur built a domed mausoleum over the 11th-century Sufi Ahmad Yasawi's grave in the 1390s, the city took the name Hazrat-i-Turkistan; it rose as capital of the Kazakh Khanate between the 16th and 18th centuries and remains a significant city, named 'Spiritual Capital of the Turkic World' in 2021.

name: Paykend
why: Wikipedia says Paykend 'was founded as a small village in the 4th century B.C.' and became 'one of the largest cities of the Bukhara oasis'. It was sacked by the Arab governor Qutayba ibn Muslim after a 706 revolt and 'never recovered from the sack', and 'the city ceased to exist in the middle of the 9th century' owing to the Zarafshan River's lower reaches becoming inaccessible. Century-level dates are approximate.

name: Akhsikath
why: Wikipedia states Akhsikath 'was established by the 3rd century BC' (approximate) and became one of the largest cities of the Fergana Valley by the 10th century, later the residence of Umar Shaikh Mirza II, Babur's father. It was sacked by the Qara Khitai and by Jebe Noyan in 1219, then 'what was left of the city was destroyed in an earthquake in 1620 and the inhabitants relocated to Namangan'.

name: Mizdakhkan
why: Wikipedia (under the title Mizdahkan) says it 'was founded in the 4th century BC, eventually becoming one of the largest cities of Khwarazm'. It records that 'Mizdahkan thrived until the 14th century when Timur led three campaigns against Khorezm. He attacked Mizdahkan and reduced it to rubble', after which 'the city was depopulated and used solely as a burial place'; the 14th-century end date is approximate given the article's own inconsistent internal dating (it elsewhere gives 1338).

name: Vardanzi
why: Wikipedia says Vardana 'was built' by a Sasanian prince, Shapur, and that the historian Narshakhi 'believed [it was] older than Bukhara, having been built in the 6th century A.D.' It was a seat of the Vardan-khudat rulers and a major border and trade town, but 'due to the translational motion of sand, in the 19th century it was bombarded by them and became uninhabitable' (exact year not given, so approximate).

name: Zamakhshar
why: Wikipedia (under the title Izmukshir) says 'Zamakhshar was a prominent town of medieval Khwarazm' and 'the birthplace of Al-Zamakhshari' (b. 1075), a Muslim polymath, but gives no explicit founding or destruction date. The from-date (medieval Khwarazm, c. 11th century) and the 1221 end-date (Mongol invasion of Khwarazm) rely on general historical knowledge rather than the extract itself, so both are flagged approximate.

name: Abiward
why: Wikipedia describes Abiward as 'an ancient Sasanian city' and a fortified border town of Greater Khorasan, noted by medieval geographers Al-Muqaddasi and the Hudud al-'Alam for its agriculture and 'warlike' frontier population. No explicit founding or destruction year is given in the extract; the Sasanian-era founding (c. 3rd century) and the 1221 Mongol destruction are drawn from general knowledge of the region's history, so both dates are approximate.

name: Margilan
why: Wikipedia says 'the settlement appeared in the II-I centuries BC, when one of the roads of Silk Road passed through Fergana', and 'the name Margilan has been known since the 10th century'. It has been 'renowned for its silk goods as far back as the 10th century' and remains a major silk-producing city today (population 253,500 in the 2024 census), so it continues; no clear end to its significance is stated.

name: Kokand
why: Wikipedia says 'the city appeared not later than the 2nd half of the 2nd century BC' and existed by the 10th century under the name Khavakand/Havokand. It became capital of the Khanate of Kokand in 1740, and Russian imperial forces 'captured the city in 1883 which then became part of Russian Turkistan', ending its role as an independent khanate capital; the city continues today (population c. 322,100 in 2022).

name: Qarshi
why: Wikipedia says Qarshi was 'originally the Sogdian city of Nakhshab', later 'the Islamic Uzbek (Turkic) city of Nasaf, and the Chagatay city of Qarshi'; Timur built a fortified palace here in 1364. An official source cited in the article's external links refers to the '2700th anniversary of Karshi', implying a founding around the 7th century BC, so the from-date is approximate and based partly on that citation rather than the main prose. It remains a regional capital today (population 278,300 in 2021).

name: Yangikent
why: Wikipedia (under the title Jankent, with Yangikent given as an alternative name) says it is 'known from Arab writings of the 10th century AD as the capital of the steppe empire of Oghuz Turks', with the earliest settlement founded 'in the 7th century by a displaced population of the Dzhetyasar culture' and the enclosed town built in the 9th or 10th century. It 'was abandoned some time between the 12th and 14th century AD', so both dates are approximate.

name: Jand
why: Wikipedia says Jand 'was the winter capital of the Seljuk Turks' and 'the historical seat of the Seljuk Dynasty from 985 to 1037' before Seljuk's tribe migrated there from the Oghuz Yabgu State; it remained under Khwarazmian rule 'until the Mongol conquest of the Central Asia in 1221', after which it was sacked and 'is now in ruins'. No explicit founding date is given, so the from-date (a pre-existing Oghuz frontier town by the 10th century) relies on general knowledge and is approximate.

name: Ordu-Baliq
why: Wikipedia states: 'In 744, after the defeat of the last Goturk Kaghan..., the Uyghurs under Bayanchur Khan...established their imperial capital Ordu Baliq...Ordu-Baliq flourished until 840, when it was reduced to ruin by the invading Yenisei Kyrgyz.' An 821 visitor, Tamim ibn Bahr, described it as 'a great town, rich in agriculture' with 'twelve iron gates of huge size'.

name: Avarga
why: Wikipedia says Avarga 'was the steppe where the first nomadic capital of the Mongol Empire was located after Genghis Khan seized the territory from the Jurkin clan', and that 'a 2020 study concluded that Avarga was Genghis Khan's winter base camp, based on radiocarbon chronology', before 'it soon proved too small and the Mongol court established the base of Karakorum'. The extract gives no exact years, so the founding (c. 1206, when the Mongol Empire was proclaimed) and end (c. 1220, when Karakorum was founded) rely on general historical knowledge and are approximate.

name: Gyeongju
why: Wikipedia: Korean records say Saro-guk 'was established in 57 BCE, when six small villages in the Gyeongju area united under Bak Hyeokgeose'; as Silla it was known as Sŏrabŏl and 'ruled about two-thirds of the Korean peninsula at its height'. Silla lasted 57 BC-935 AD; the Goryeo-era rename to Gyeongju and the exact Sŏrabŏl/Silla naming transition are approximate, as is the traditional founding year itself.

name: Gongju
why: Wikipedia: 'Gongju was formerly named Ungjin and was the capital of Baekje from AD 475 to 538 ... In 538, King Seong moved the capital to Sabi.' Gongju remained an important Baekje centre afterwards. The exact year the town's name changed to Gongju is not given, so that date is approximate.

name: Buyeo
why: Wikipedia: 'Buyeo-eup, the county's capital, was the site of the capital of Baekje from 538-660 AD, during which it was called Sabi.' Sabi fell with Baekje in 660; the exact year the site came to be called Buyeo is not stated, so it is approximate.

name: Kaesong
why: Wikipedia: 'when a castle was built at the site in 694 ... Kaesong was referred to as Song'ak', with the name assumed in use somewhat earlier; 'In 919, Kaesong became the national capital' under Goryeo founder Wang Geon. Kaesong's status as national capital ended in 1392 when Joseon moved the capital south, a fact not in the extract but well established generally (approximate).

name: Gungnae
why: Wikipedia: 'Gungnae was chosen to become the capital city by the ruler Yuri during the 10th month of the year 3 AD' and 'Gungnae City fell to the Silla-Tang Chinese alliance when General Yŏn Namsaeng ... surrendered the city in 666.' The nearby mountain fortress Hwando (the candidate's name hint) is described on Wikipedia as built to protect this capital, so Gungnae itself is used as the capital-city entry, near Ji'an on the China/North Korea border.

name: Ganghwa Island
why: Wikipedia: 'Goryeogung is a palace site of Goryeo from 1232 to 1270 in Incheon'; the Ganghwa County article adds that 'the court of Goryeo took refuge on the island as Mongol forces invaded in 1232 ... After Goryeo capitulated to the Mongols, the elite forces on the island rose up and began the Sambyeolcho Rebellion,' with the court leaving the island around 1270.

name: Nara
why: Wikipedia: 'Nara was the capital of Japan during the Nara period from 710 to 784 as the seat of the Emperor before the capital was moved to Nagaoka-kyō'; the Heijō-kyō article adds that 'Empress Genmei ordered the Imperial capital moved from Fujiwara-kyō to Heijō-kyō in 708, and the move to Heijō-kyō was complete in 710.'

name: Nagaoka-kyō
why: Wikipedia: 'Nagaoka-kyō (長岡京) was the capital of Japan from 784 to 794 ... built by order of Emperor Kanmu.' Coordinates taken from Wikidata (Q1052803) as the English article carries no coordinate tag.

name: Fujiwara-kyō
why: Wikipedia: 'Fujiwara-kyō (藤原京) was the Imperial capital of Japan for sixteen years, between 694 and 710 ... having been moved from nearby Asuka, and remained the capital until its relocation to Heijō-kyō.'

name: Ōtsu
why: Wikipedia: 'From 667 to 672, the Ōmi Ōtsu Palace, founded by Emperor Tenji, was the capital of Japan. Following the Jinshin War Ōtsu was renamed Furutsu ... With the establishment of the new capital [Heian-kyō, 794], the name of the city was restored to Ōtsu.'

name: Dazaifu
why: Wikipedia: 'A fortified site that was the imperial office governing Kyūshū ... was established in 663 AD, and the name "Dazaifu" first appears in the Nihon Shoki in 671 AD.' Under the Taiho Code (701) it administered Kyushu and received foreign embassies, but 'the government offices were burned down during the rebellion of Fujiwara no Sumitomo in 941 and with the decline of imperial authority, Dazaifu never regained its earlier prestige.' The exact founding year (663 vs 671) is approximate.

name: Kamakura
why: Wikipedia: 'Kamakura was Japan's de facto capital when it was the seat of the Kamakura shogunate from 1185 to 1333, established by Minamoto no Yoritomo. It was the first military government in Japan's history.'

name: Sakai
why: Wikipedia: 'Medieval Sakai was an autonomous city governed by merchant oligarchs. During the late Muromachi period and the Sengoku period, from about 1450 to 1600, Sakai developed into one of the richest cities in Japan as a center of foreign trade.' By the 1530s its population had reached about 40,000.

name: Hiraizumi
why: Wikipedia: 'In about 1100, Fujiwara no Kiyohira moved his home ... to Mount Kanzan in Hiraizumi', where the Northern Fujiwara clan ruled as de facto capital of Ōshū 'for about 100 years'. 'Hiraizumi's golden age lasted for nearly 100 years. It was destroyed in 1189.' The founding year is given only as 'about 1100'.

name: Ichijōdani
why: Wikipedia: 'In 1471 ... Asakura Toshikage fortified the Ichijōdani by constructing hilltop fortifications ... and eventually [it hosted] the residences of merchants and artisans, and Buddhist temples,' reaching 'a peak population of over 10,000 inhabitants.' 'Ichijōdani was razed to the ground by Nobunaga during the 1573 Siege of Ichijōdani Castle.'

name: Kusado Sengen
why: Wikipedia: 'Kusado Sengen ... is the name of a medieval town in Japan ... a minor commercial port town on the Seto Inland Sea during the Kamakura and Muromachi periods,' known only from excavation (discovered 1961) rather than documentary founding/abandonment dates. Dates here are approximated to the span of the Kamakura and Muromachi periods (c.1185-1573).

name: Yoshinogari
why: Wikipedia: Yoshinogari is 'a large and complex Yayoi period archaeological site ... dates back to between the 3rd century BC and the 3rd century AD,' with 'recent attempts to use absolute dating methods such as AMS radiocarbon dating' showing 'the earliest Yayoi component of Yoshinogari dates back to before 400 BC.' It was a large moated settlement with watchtowers, dwellings and communal cemeteries; dates are approximate ranges rather than exact years.

name: Yamaguchi
why: Wikipedia: 'During the Muromachi period it was ruled by the Ōuchi clan, who at their height ruled over six provinces ... After the Ōnin War, they welcomed intellectuals who escaped from Kyoto, such that Yamaguchi prospered as a center of culture ... The Ōuchi were eventually overthrown by their vassals, the Mōri clan.' The extract gives no exact years for the Ōuchi seat or its fall; the mid-14th-century move to Yamaguchi and the Mōri takeover completed by 1557 are added from general knowledge (approximate).

name: Odawara
why: Wikipedia (Odawara Castle article): the Omori clan of Suruga 'were in turn defeated by Ise Moritoki [Hōjō Sōun] of Izu, founder of the Odawara Hōjō clan in 1495.' The Odawara article adds: 'During the Sengoku period, Odawara developed as a castle town and capital of the domains of the later Hōjō clan ... The Hōjō were defeated by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in the Battle of Odawara in 1590.'

name: Shigatse
why: Wikipedia's article on the district (Samzhubzê, Xigazê) says Shigatse began urbanising in the 11th century during the Sakya dynasty and became capital of Ü-Tsang province, with the Shigatse Dzong later serving as seat of the kings of Ü-Tsang; the Shigatse article calls it Tibet's second-largest city and the historic seat of the Panchen Lama at Tashilhunpo Monastery (founded 1447), a role that continues today. Century given only as "11th century", so from is a midpoint estimate.

name: Gyantse
why: Wikipedia describes Gyantse as historically the third largest and most prominent town in Tibet, strategically sited on the ancient trade routes from the Chumbi Valley, Yatung and Sikkim; its fortress guarding the approaches to Lhasa was built in 1390. The town hosted a British trade agent and garrison from 1904 to 1947, but declined after the 1954 flood and the 1959 unrest and Cultural Revolution, which saw the Palcho Monastery and Kumbum ransacked. It still exists as a town, so heyday-end year (1959) is an estimate rather than a quoted date.

name: Sakya
why: Sakya Monastery, founded in 1073 by Khön Könchok Gyalpo, is described as "situated in Sa'gya Town, Sa'gya County", confirming a town exists around/with the monastery today. The separate Wikipedia article on the Sakya school states Sakya lamas and Imperial Preceptors "continued to serve as viceroys or administrators of Tibet on behalf of Yuan emperors for nearly 75 years after Phagpa's death in 1280, until the Yuan dynasty was greatly weakened by the Red Turban Rebellion in the 1350s" — i.e. Sakya's period as de facto seat of Tibetan government under Yuan patronage ran to roughly 1354, when the Phagmodrupa dynasty took over. No dedicated Wikipedia article exists for the town itself, so no Wikidata id is given; founding and end dates are estimated from the monastery/school history.

name: Tsaparang
why: Tsaparang was made capital of the Kingdom of Guge after the assassination of Langdarma (838-841 CE) and the Tibetan Empire's break-up; other accounts say two of Langdarma's grandsons fled to western Tibet "about 919 CE", with Guge emerging as an independent kingdom soon after. Wikipedia describes Tsaparang as a fortress-village with a settlement of common people at its base, temples and a royal citadel. It hosted Jesuit missionaries from 1624. In 1630 the king of Ladakh "invaded and overthrew the kingdom of Guge", and in 1679-80 "Tsaparang and the Guge kingdom were conquered by Central Tibet", after which it was abandoned; described as an "Abandoned settlement in Tibet". Founding date is approximate (only "about 919 CE" and a 10th-century emergence given).

name: Nedong
why: Wikipedia states "Nedong was the seat of the Phagmodrupa dynasty, which was the dominating regime in Tibet from 1354 to 1435 and maintained a degree of authority until the early 17th century." The village survives today (Q665203), and the wider area is now Shannan's Nêdong District, so it continues; the heyday-end year is an estimated midpoint of "early 17th century".

name: Tosaminato
why: Wikipedia describes Tosaminato as "a port settlement which existed from the Heian to the Muromachi period", developed as a trade centre with the Ainu and the Asian mainland "by the Hiraizumi-based Northern Fujiwara during the Heian period" (from is a midpoint estimate for that period). From 1229 it came under the Andō clan, who dominated trade with Ezo, and by the early Muromachi period it was a major Sea of Japan coastal port also trading directly with Korea. It declined rapidly after the Andō clan was forced out by Nanbu clan attacks in 1432, and the harbour eventually silted up; excavations show its apogee was the later 14th to early 15th century.

name: Chaoge
why: Wikipedia: capital of the State of Wey during the Western Zhou period, located in modern Qi County, Hebi. The Wey (state) article records that Rong peoples "successfully attacked the capital at Zhaoge, killing the Duke" in the eighth year of Duke Yi's reign (660 BCE), after which the capital moved to Chuqiu; the founding date is approximated to Wey's early Western Zhou enfeoffment centred on Zhaoge, the former Shang capital.

name: Puyang
why: The Wey (state) article records that by 320 BCE "Wey controlled only the county of Puyang" and that in 241 BCE "Qin captured Puyang during its attack on Wei, incorporating it into the new Dong Commandery", ending Wey's tenure there; Puyang's own article records Cao Cao's headquarters there 191-196 CE and its Yangshao-era heritage. The exact year Wey's capital moved to Puyang (traditionally Diqiu) is approximated from general historical knowledge, not directly quoted.

name: Shangcai
why: The Cai (state) article: Cai Shu Du "was enfeoffed at present-day Shangcai ('Upper Cai') in Henan" at the beginning of the Zhou dynasty, and invasions from Chu "relocated Cai several times, first to Xincai... in 531 BC", ending Shangcai's status as capital. Shangcai County's own article confirms it as the site of the ancient Cai state.

name: Jiayuguan
why: Named after the nearby Jiayu Pass, "the largest and most intact pass of the Great Wall of China", with the fortress "situated at the end of the portion of the Great Wall... built by the Ming Dynasty in the 14th century." Wikipedia's city article mainly documents the modern settlement (county-level city established 1965 around the Jiuquan Iron and Steel Works, prefecture-level from 1971); continuity of a smaller garrison/civilian town at the pass between the Ming fort and the 20th-century city relies on general historical knowledge rather than a direct quote, so the founding year is approximated to the mid-14th century.

name: Suoyang City
why: "First established as Ming'an County in 111 BC by Emperor Wu of Han, the city was relocated and rebuilt at the current site in 295 AD... As the capital of Jinchang Commandery... the city prospered during the Tang and Western Xia dynasties... It was destroyed and abandoned in the 16th century, after the Ming dynasty came under attack by Mansur Khan of Moghulistan", roughly two decades after wall repairs recorded in 1494. Called Kuyu under the Ming from 1405; the name Suoyang City derives from a later Qing-dynasty novel.

name: Bunjikat
why: "The archaeological site of Bunjikat is the location of the former capital of the Principality of Ushrusana." The Osrushana article records the principality's afshin dynasty ruling "until 280 AH/893 AD (coin of the last ruler Sayr b. Abdallah of 279 [892])", after which "the country became a province of the Samanids and ceased to have an independent existence." The town's earlier founding date is approximated from general knowledge of Ustrushana's urbanisation out of Sogdiana, not directly quoted. The modern populated jamoat of the same name has a different administrative seat (Guliston), so the ancient capital itself is treated as extinct.

name: Kath
why: "Beruniy was the capital of Khwarezm from the time of the Afrighid dynasty around 305 CE, replacing the old capital of Toprak-Kala. At that time it was known as Kath." It was later known as Fil and Shobboz, and renamed Beruniy in 1957 after the scholar Al-Biruni, who was born there; the city continues today with a population of 55,900 (2016). The year Kath lost its status as Khwarazm's capital to Gurganj (Urgench) is not given in the extract and is approximated from general knowledge, commonly placed around the late 10th century.

name: Gimhae
why: Gimhae "is the seat of the large Gimhae Kim clan... claiming descent from the ancient royal house of Geumgwan Gaya." The Geumgwan Gaya article describes it as "the ruling city-state of the Gaya confederacy that existed from 43 to 532 CE... believed to have been located around the modern-day city of Gimhae", ending when it "capitulated to Silla in 532 AD."

name: Goryeong
why: "Goryeong is a historical center of the ancient kingdom of Daegaya." The Daegaya article records the state "existed for about 520 years from the first king, Ijinasi... to the last, Doseolji" and that "Daegaya fell to the armies of Silla under general Kim Isabu in 562"; the founding year is derived from the stated 520-year span ending in 562.

name: Jungwon-gyeong
why: Chungju's own Wikipedia article does not mention its status as one of Silla's five secondary capitals; this is drawn from general historical knowledge - that Jungwon-gyeong was established under King Sinmun of Silla around 685 CE and lost its special status when renamed Chungju under Goryeo around 940 CE - and is not a direct quote. Wikipedia does confirm the site's later history, including the 1592 Battle of Chungju during Hideyoshi's invasions of Korea.

name: Bugwon-gyeong
why: Wonju's Wikipedia article records that "during the time of Great Joseon, Wonju was the capital of the historic Gangwon Province", a long administrative significance. Its earlier role as Bugwon-gyeong, one of Silla's five secondary capitals established under King Sinmun around 685 CE, and the approximate year its provincial-capital status ended (Gangwon's capital moving elsewhere in the 1890s), are drawn from general historical knowledge rather than quoted directly from this extract.

name: Namwon-gyeong
why: "Namwon was founded in 680 during the reign of King Sinmun of Silla Kingdom" - consistent with its historical role as Namwon-gyeong, one of Silla's five secondary capitals. The city later suffered the 1597 Siege of Namwon during the Imjin War, when "the only defenders against the Japanese army of 56,000 men were 3300 Korean and Chinese soldiers and 6000 women and children", but continues today. The year its status as a Silla secondary capital ended is approximated from general knowledge (Silla-Goryeo administrative reforms, c. 940), not directly quoted.

name: Tagajō
why: "In 729 AD, a large fortified settlement, Taga Castle, was established by the imperial dynasty as a military center... The fortification became the administrative capital of Mutsu Province under the Ritsuryō system. The tsunami in 869 caused extensive flooding of the Sendai plain, destroying the town of Tagajō." The settlement continues today as the city of Tagajō, designated a city in 1971.

name: Akita
why: "During the Nara period, the imperial court established Akita Castle in 733 AD to bring the local Emishi tribes under its control", serving as a frontier provincial headquarters of Dewa Province. Wikipedia does not state when Akita Castle's administrative role ended before the area came under local samurai clans in the Sengoku period; this is approximated to the early 9th century from general historical knowledge. The settlement continues today as Akita, capital of Akita Prefecture.

name: Sanxingdui
why: Wikipedia: archaeological digs 'showed evidence of a walled city founded c. 1,600 BCE', identified with the ancient kingdom of Shu; the trapezoidal walls enclosed 3.6 sq km. The Sanxingdui culture (periods II-III) 'is contemporaneous with the Shang dynasty'; its end (natural disaster or invasion) is placed here at approximately 1046 BCE, matching the fall of Shang (approx).

name: Liangzhu
why: Used the dedicated 'Archaeological ruins of Liangzhu City' article, distinct from the broader 'Liangzhu culture' article, since it specifically describes the walled city site: 'Existing from approximately 3300 to 2300 BCE, the city was ultimately abandoned' due to flooding linked to climate change. Confirmed as an ancient city after the 2006 discovery of its walls; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019.

name: Taosi
why: Wikipedia dates the 'late phase of the Longshan culture in southern Shanxi, also known as the Taosi phase (2300 BC to 1900 BC)'. The rammed-clay enclosure had an inner area of 280 ha and East Asia's oldest known astronomical observatory; some archaeologists identify it as the capital of Emperor Yao's state of Tang, and 'it is theorized that the city collapsed with a rebellion against the ruling class.'

name: Shimao
why: Wikipedia: Shimao 'is dated to around 2000 BC, near the end of the Longshan period, and is the largest known walled site of that period in China, at 400 ha'; abandonment is tied to 'a rapid shift to a cooler, drier climate on the Loess Plateau, from around 2000 to 1700 BC'. The wider occupation span (c. 2300-1800 BCE) used here draws on general knowledge beyond the quoted extract (approx).

name: Chengtoushan
why: Wikipedia: the walls and moat were 'built around 4000 BC' (clamped to -3400; true founding date is earlier, approx), making Chengtoushan 'possibly one of the oldest walled sites in China', existing 'for two millennia'. The settlement spanned the Daxi, Qujialing and Shijiahe cultures and 'was abandoned around the middle period of the Shijiahe culture' (approx).

name: Jimo
why: Wikipedia: 'Jimo was established in the Eastern Zhou dynasty, at which time it was the second largest settlement in Shandong' (approx -770, start of Eastern Zhou). It withstood the 'Siege of Jimo in 279 BC', famous for Tian Dan's fire-oxen ruse that restored Qi's fortunes; its ancient significance is set here as ending with Qin's conquest of Qi in 221 BCE (approx). It continues today as a district of Qingdao.

name: Zoucheng
why: Wikipedia: Mencius 'was born in Zoucheng, then within the feudal State of Zou', and his descendants 'lived in Zoucheng all the way to the present'; the Mencius Temple's 'history dates back to the year 1037' (Northern Song). The State of Zou's founding (c. 11th century BCE Western Zhou enfeoffment) and its later annexation by Chu (c. 3rd century BCE) are not in the extract and rely on general knowledge (approx).

name: Huaiyang
why: Wikipedia: 'In ancient times, it was known as Wanqiu, Chen, and even Chen State. During the Qin Dynasty, it was assigned to Chen Commandery', later reorganised into Huaiyang Commandery in the early Western Han. The precise founding of the State of Chen (c. 1046 BCE, Western Zhou enfeoffment) and its conquest by Chu (478 BCE) are not in the extract and rely on general knowledge (approx).

name: Iksan
why: Wikipedia confirms 'Iksan was once the capital of the ancient Baekje Kingdom. Temples built then are still standing', but gives no dates. The King Mu attempted-capital period (r. 600-641 CE) named in the candidate brief is from general knowledge, not the extract (approx).

name: Sarakhs
why: Wikipedia: 'Turkmen historians consider the city to have been founded in 507 BCE', though this 'is considered to be a somewhat arbitrary choice of date' (approx); 'in its 11th century heyday had many libraries'. In 1221 the Mongols 'plundered and destroyed' Sarakhs, causing 'the temporary cease of the city's existence' before it was later rebuilt; it continues today, split by the Iran-Turkmenistan border since the 1881 Treaty of Akhal.

name: Toprak-Kala
why: Wikipedia: Toprak-Kala 'was an ancient palace city and the capital of... Chorasmia in the 2nd/3rd century CE', 'built by Artav (Artabanos), ruler of Khwarezm, in the 1st or 2nd century CE' (approx -> 100 CE). 'The location of the Chorasmian capital was changed to Kyat... sometime after 305 CE, but the town of Toprak-Kala continued to prosper until the 6th century CE' (approx 550).

name: Kanka
why: Wikipedia: 'The city appeared in the 4th century B.C.' (approx -350) and 'was identified by the Greek sources with Antihiey Zayaksartskoy'; it became 'a first capital of Chach' under the Kanguy state, with monumental fortification walls enclosing more than 160 hectares. It later became 'a second... economic and cultural center of Shash in the Middle Age' as Tashkent rose, with excavated strata from 'the 6th-7th and 11th-12th centuries' (approx end 1150). A distinct site from Tashkent, about 80 km southwest of it per the article.

name: Tsuruga
why: Wikipedia: 'A settlement at Tsuruga is mentioned in the Nara period Kojiki and Nihon Shoki chronicles' (approx 8th century CE, though the settlement predates the chronicles). It 'prospered as a major port on the kitamaebune shipping routes between western Japan and Hokkaido', was declared 'an open port for trading with the United States and the United Kingdom' in 1899, and received Polish orphans (1920) and Jewish refugees (1940) as 'the only Japanese port opened' to them, before 'much of the city centre was destroyed in 1945' by wartime bombing.

name: Onomichi
why: Wikipedia: 'The port of Onomichi opened in 1168, serving for the next five centuries as a significant rice shipment center and a hub for foreign trade. While its commercial importance shifted during the Edo period, it remained a vital maritime location.' Incorporated as a city in 1898; famous for its temples (Senko-ji, founded 9th century) and film locations.

name: Manching
why: Wikipedia 'Manching': 'In the late Iron Age, there was a Celtic settlement, the Oppidum of Manching, on the location of present-day Manching.' The oppidum's growth (3rd-1st c. BC) and abandonment around 50 BC are from general archaeological knowledge, not stated as exact years on the page (approx).

name: Heuneburg
why: Wikipedia 'Heuneburg': 'reoccupied and refortified around 700 BC... by 600 BC, it was one of the key centres of power and trade... Before 500 BC, the site suffered a major destruction, followed by a second flourish and a further destruction in the 5th century BC.' Called 'oldest city north of the Alps' and identified with Herodotus's Pyrene.

name: Alcimoennis
why: Wikipedia 'Alcimoennis': 'The oppidum dates to the late La Tène period... it is estimated that it was abandoned some time around the middle of the first century BCE.' Celtic hillfort/oppidum above modern Kelheim, Bavaria; possibly the Vindelici's central settlement.

name: Třísov
why: Wikipedia 'Holubov' (the modern municipality including Třísov): 'The Celts lived in the area from about 200-400 BC, and in about 60 BC they founded an oppidum in Třísov... they left the place in around 60 BC being pushed out from here by migrating Marcomanni tribe.' The page's own founding/leaving dates appear to be a typo (both given as 60 BC); from is estimated (approx) as preceding the recorded departure.

name: Dünsberg
why: Wikipedia 'Dünsberg': 'Fortification systems of the hill are detectable from the Urnfield period (8th century BC). The outer ramparts of the hillfort had 14 gates. The Celtic settlement (oppidum) reached its height during the La Tène period (about the 3rd century BC).' No abandonment year given on the page; end estimated from general knowledge of Hessian oppida decline (approx).

name: Alesia
why: Wikipedia 'Alesia (city)': 'Alesia was the capital of the Mandubii... The Celtic oppidum was conquered by Julius Caesar during the Gallic Wars and afterwards became a Gallo-Roman town.' Entry covers the independent Celtic oppidum only; the subsequent Gallo-Roman town is Pleiades territory. Founding date approximate.

name: Hedeby
why: Wikipedia 'Hedeby': first mentioned in Frankish chronicles under 804; 'Hedeby was abandoned after its destruction in 1066.' Trade shifted to nearby Schleswig, founded on the other side of the Schlei.

name: Birka
why: Wikipedia 'Birka': 'Birka was founded around AD 750 and it flourished for more than 200 years. It was abandoned c. AD 975, around the same time Sigtuna was founded as a Christian town some 35 km to the northeast.'

name: Kaupang
why: Wikipedia 'Kaupang': 'Kaupang is the site of the remains of one of Scandinavia's earliest urban sites, established in year 800. Kaupang was abandoned in the mid-10th century.' First known Norwegian trading outpost.

name: Ribe
why: Wikipedia 'Ribe': 'It is the oldest town in Denmark.' The page does not give the exact Viking-age emporium founding year (traditionally c. 704-710, from general knowledge, approx); the town continues today as a small Danish town, no longer the major trading centre it was in the Viking age.

name: Truso
why: Wikipedia 'Truso': 'The beginnings of the town has been dated back to approximately the end of the 7th century... in the second half of the 10th century siltation in the Nogat had begun to cut off the town... importance as trading port began to decline and was eventually eclipsed by the ascent of Gdańsk.' Site near Elbląg (Janów Pomorski), coordinates approximate.

name: Wolin
why: Wikipedia 'Wolin (town)': 'Dating from the 9th century, it has been associated with the semi-legendary settlements of Jomsburg, Jumne, Julin and Vineta... The early medieval town fell victim to the late 12th century Danish raids, and was refounded in 1260.' A small modern town of the same name continues on the site.

name: Staraya Ladoga
why: Wikipedia 'Staraya Ladoga': 'Dendrochronology suggests that Ladoga was founded in 753... sometimes called the first capital of Russia.' 'By the end of the 15th century, it had lost all of its importance.' Continues today as a rural locality (selo), formerly Ladoga proper, renamed Staraya (Old) Ladoga in 1704.

name: Gnezdovo
why: Wikipedia 'Gnezdovo': 'contains extensive remains of a Slavic-Varangian settlement that flourished in the 10th century as a major trade station on the trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks.' Predecessor site to Smolensk; founding approximate.

name: Sarkel
why: Wikipedia 'Sarkel': built by the Khazars with Byzantine help, 'Sarkel was built to protect the north-western border of the Khazar state in 833.' Captured by Sviatoslav I in 965 and renamed Belaya Vezha, 'remained Slavic until the 12th century, when the district was taken over by the Kipchaks.' Site now under the Tsimlyansk Reservoir.

name: Atil
why: Wikipedia 'Atil': 'Atil, also Itil, was the capital of the Khazar Khaganate from the mid-8th century to the late 10th century... Its precise location has long been unknown' (a 2008 claimed discovery near Astrakhan 'has since been disproven'). Destruction year (969) is from general knowledge of Sviatoslav's campaign against Khazaria, not stated on the page (approx); coordinates are an approximate Volga-delta placement, flagged approx.

name: Bolghar
why: Wikipedia 'Bolghar': 'intermittently the capital of Volga Bulgaria from the 10th to the 13th centuries'; sacked by Mongols in 1236 and by Bulat-Timur in 1361, but 'persevered until the mid-16th century when the Khanate of Kazan was conquered by the Russian Tsar Ivan IV.' A small modern town called Bolgar has existed to the west since 1991.

name: Bilär
why: Wikipedia 'Bilär': 'founded around 10th century by the indigenous Bilär tribe... served as the capital of Volga Bulgaria in the 12th and 13th centuries. In 1236, the city was sacked by the army of Batu Khan... it never regained its former size or power.'

name: Suar
why: Wikipedia 'Suar, Volga Bulgaria': 'a medieval (9th-14th century) Volga Bulgarian city, the capital of Suar Principality in 948-975... After the Mongol invasion of Volga Bulgaria in 1236 the city lost its importance.' The page notes scholarly disagreement over the exact site; coordinates approximate.

name: Cükätaw
why: Wikipedia 'Cükätaw' (also Juketau/Zhukotin): 'a medieval Bolgar city during the 10th to 15th centuries CE... capital of the Cükätaw Duchy. In 1236 Cükätaw was destroyed by Batu Khan's troops... After the town was sacked by Yuri of Zvenigorod in 1414, it was abandoned.' Coordinates approximate (near modern Chistopol).

name: Tmutarakan
why: Wikipedia 'Tmutarakan': Khazar fortress of Tamantarkhan built on the site in the 7th century; 'became known as Tmutarakan when it came under the control of Kievan Rus'' 'between the late 10th and 11th centuries.' Entry covers the Khazar/Rus phase only; the earlier Greek colony Hermonassa on the same site is Pleiades territory. End date approximate.

name: Kaup
why: Wikipedia 'Kaup (emporium)': 'a major center of Old Prussians sprang up there in the early 9th century... Kaup flourished as a market town protected by a garrison until the end of the 10th century,' then was 'burned to the ground by the Dane Cnut the Great during his anti-Prussian raid in 1016... The Norsemen's raids ended in the 11th century... but the Prussians continued to occupy the site until the Northern Crusades of the 13th century.' Successor to Grobiņa and Truso as the leading Amber Road emporium.

name: Grobiņa
why: Wikipedia 'Grobiņa': 'the most important political centre on the territory of Latvia' in the Early Middle Ages, 'comparable in many ways to Hedeby and Birka but probably predating them both'; as Seeburg it was 'pillaged, ravaged, and burnt by the Swedes' c. 854 after a Curonian revolt. A Latvian town of the same name (chartered 1695) stands on the site today.

name: Apuolė
why: Wikipedia 'Apuolė': 'Having survived a viking attack in 854, Apuolė is the oldest Lithuanian settlement mentioned in written sources.' Besieged for eight days by Swedes per the Vita Ansgari but not taken. A small village of the same name exists today.

name: Kernavė
why: Wikipedia 'Kernavė': 'first mentioned in 1279... In 1390... the knights burned the town and its buildings... After this raid, the town wasn't rebuilt.' Called 'the first capital of Lithuania'; founding predates the 1279 mention (approx).

name: Senieji Trakai
why: Wikipedia 'Senieji Trakai': 'Sometime before 1321, Grand Duke Gediminas transferred the capital of Lithuania from Kernavė to Trakai (today's Senieji Trakai)... The castle in Senieji Trakai was destroyed by the Teutonic Order in 1391.' A village of the same name (Old Trakai) exists on the site today.

name: Semender
why: Wikipedia's 'Semender' article covers only the unrelated modern urban locality (established 1999); it does not describe the historic Khazar capital. This entry for the Khazar city of Semender (an early Khazar capital before Atil, said to have been sacked in Sviatoslav's 968-969 campaign) relies on general knowledge, not the Wikipedia page, and is flagged approx accordingly.

name: Ukek
why: Wikipedia 'Ukek': 'Probably established in the 1240s, Ukek became an important trade center by the early 14th century.' 'Timur's troops sacked the city in 1395.' Ibn Battuta called it 'a city of middling size, with fine buildings.'

name: Saqsin
why: Wikipedia 'Saqsin': 'a medieval city that flourished from the eleventh to the thirteenth centuries... known in pre-Mongol times as Saksin-Bolgar, which in Mongol times became Sarai Batu.' Location and exact end date uncertain (approx); coordinates approximate, Volga delta.

name: Sarai Batu
why: Wikipedia 'Sarai (city)', 'Old Sarai' section: established by Batu Khan (r. 1227-1255); William of Rubruck's 1253/54 account is 'considered the first historical reference to the city.' Timur 'sacked, leveled, and set on fire Sarai in the winter of 1395-1396.' The page notes 'considerable disagreement among scholars' about the site; coordinates approximate.

name: New Sarai
why: Wikipedia 'Sarai (city)', 'New Sarai' section: founded by Öz Beg Khan, formal founding placed at '1334-1335'; sacked by Timur in the winter of 1395-1396, partially recovered, then 'Sarai was plundered by the ushkuyniki, riverine pirates from Vyatka, in 1471.' Site identification disputed; coordinates approximate.

name: Azaq
why: Wikipedia 'Azov': 'The Kipchaks, seizing the area in 1067, renamed it Azaq... The Golden Horde claimed most of the coast in the 13th and 14th centuries, but Venetian and Genoese merchants... founded there a colony which they called Tana.' In 1471 the Ottomans built the fortress of Azak, converting the trading town into a military stronghold. Continues today as the Russian town of Azov.

name: Majar
why: Wikipedia 'Majar (Golden Horde)': 'a medieval city of Golden Horde in 13th-14th centuries... In 1310-1311 the city minted its own money. In 1395 it was sacked by troops of Timur.' Visited by Ibn Battuta c. 1332, who called it 'a large town, one of the finest of the cities of the Turks.'

name: İske Qazan
why: Wikipedia 'İske Qazan': 'a Bolghar-Tatar city in the 13-16th centuries... one of the political and economic centres of Kazan artı' in the 13th-14th centuries; declined after Russian raids of 1376 and 1399; 'In 1552 İske Kazan was ruined by Russian troops.' Coordinates approximate.

name: Staryi Krym
why: Wikipedia 'Staryi Krym': 'probably the site of an earlier Khazar fortress before the Mongol conquest of the Crimea in mid-1238... became a capital of the Crimean Yurt.' Capital of the Crimean Khanate moved to Bağçasaray in 1532, after which 'the city declined into relative obscurity.' A small modern city of the same Russian name continues on the site.

name: Gelonus
why: Wikipedia 'Bilsk hillfort': 'a hillfort of the Scythian period (end of 8th to beginning of 3rd centuries BC)... At that time, Europe had no settlements or fortifications larger than those. A number of scholars identify the Bilsk site with the Scythian city of Gelonus, which is mentioned by Herodotus (though this view has been disputed).' Coordinates approximate (near Bilsk, Poltava Oblast).

name: Scythian Neapolis
why: Wikipedia 'Scythian Neapolis': 'existed in the Crimean Peninsula from the end of the 3rd century BC until the second half of the 3rd century AD... regarded as the capital of the Late Scythian Kingdom and the capital of Great Scythia,' led by Skilurus and Palacus.

name: Mikulčice
why: Wikipedia 'Mikulčice-Valy': 'Settlement started possibly in the 8th century AD and continued until the demise of the Great Moravia Empire into the early part [of the] 10th century.' One of Great Moravia's principal fortified settlements, with an 'Acropolis' and several churches; located 3 km from the modern village of Mikulčice.

name: Pohansko
why: Wikipedia 'Břeclav', history section: 'In the late 8th century, a large Slavic gord, today called Pohansko... was established southeast of today's town. In the 9th century, it became a significant centre of Great Moravia... It was abandoned in the 10th century.'

name: Staré Město
why: Wikipedia 'Staré Město (Uherské Hradiště District)': 'The area of Staré Město was inhabited already in the 9th century, during the era of the Great Moravian Empire.' A modern town of about 6,700 inhabitants stands on the site.

name: Devín
why: Wikipedia 'Devín Castle': possibly mentioned in 864 as the 'castle of Dowina' besieged by Louis the German; 'During the Great Moravian period, Devín was the center of a larger agglomeration,' with a pre-Romanesque church built c. 850-870. Now a borough of Bratislava.

name: Old Sarum
why: Wikipedia 'Old Sarum': 'the ruined and deserted site of the earliest settlement of Salisbury'; a hillfort from c. 400 BC, occupied through Roman and Saxon periods, with a Norman cathedral and castle. The move of the cathedral to New Salisbury in 1226 and the town's eventual desertion are on the page; the final abandonment year (c. 1331, when New Salisbury received the old town's building stone) is from general knowledge (approx).

name: Dunwich
why: Wikipedia 'Dunwich': 'In the Anglo-Saxon period, Dunwich was the capital of the Kingdom of the East Angles... Its decline began in 1286 when a storm surge hit the East Anglian coast, followed by two great storms in February and December of 1287, until it eventually shrank to the village it is today.'

name: Winchelsea
why: Wikipedia 'Winchelsea': 'The current town, which was founded in 1288, replaced an earlier town of the same name, known as Old Winchelsea, that was lost to coastal erosion in the late medieval period.' The 1287 storms that struck Dunwich also damaged Old Winchelsea (approx).

name: Ravenser Odd
why: Wikipedia 'Ravenser Odd': 'founded by the Count of Aumale in the mid-13th century,' granted a borough charter by 1299, 'more important... than Kingston upon Hull'; 'As the sandbanks shifted the town was swept away.' The final storm destruction (c. 1362, the same Grote Mandrenke that destroyed Rungholt) is from general knowledge (approx).

name: Kenfig
why: Wikipedia 'Kenfig': 'a village and former borough in Bridgend, Wales.' The page gives no dates; the Norman borough's founding (c. 1140s) and its slow burial by sand dunes through the later Middle Ages are from general knowledge (approx). A small village of the same name remains.

name: Trellech
why: Wikipedia 'Trellech': 'a relatively small village in modern times, it was one of the largest towns in Wales in the 13th century.' Its 1291 destruction during a feudal dispute (the 'Despenser War' period) is from general knowledge, not stated on the page (approx).

name: Roxburgh
why: Wikipedia 'Roxburgh': 'an important trading burgh in High Medieval to early modern Scotland... had at least as much importance as Edinburgh, Stirling, Perth, or Berwick-upon-Tweed, for a time acting as de facto capital.' Its destruction in 1460 (during the siege at which James II was killed) is from general knowledge, not stated on the page (approx).

name: Bannow
why: Wikipedia 'Bannow': 'in Norman times there was a borough called Bannow on Bannow Island at the mouth of the bay. This town has since disappeared, possibly due to the silting up of the natural harbour channels in the 14th century.' The parish and village of Bannow continue nearby under the same name.

name: Rindoon
why: Wikipedia 'Rindoon': 'an abandoned village located in County Roscommon, Ireland' -- the page gives no history. Rindoon (Rinn Dúin) was an Anglo-Norman walled town founded c. 1227 by the Justiciar of Ireland on a peninsula in Lough Ree, abandoned after repeated Irish raids by the 14th century; this is from general knowledge, not the Wikipedia page (approx).

name: Newtown Jerpoint
why: Wikipedia 'Newtown Jerpoint': 'The medieval lost town of Newtown Jerpoint is just west of the Cistercian Jerpoint Abbey.' The page gives no decline date; a 17th-century abandonment (after Cromwellian-era wars and plague) is from general knowledge (approx).

name: Gniezno
why: Wikipedia 'Gniezno': 'The ducal stronghold was founded just before 940... it was the first historical capital of Poland in the 10th century and early 11th century.' 'The cities of Gniezno and nearby Poznań were captured, plundered and destroyed in 1038 by the Bohemian duke Bretislav I, which pushed the next Polish rulers to move the Polish capital to Kraków.' Continues today as a city of about 67,000, no longer the political capital.

name: Kruszwica
why: Wikipedia 'Kruszwica': 'Initially founded in the 6th century, Kruszwica is the oldest town in the region.' A legendary early Piast/Polan stronghold; no single decline date is given on the page, so 1300 (its eclipse by Gniezno, Poznań and Kraków) is a general estimate (approx). Continues today as a small town.

name: Giecz
why: Wikipedia 'Giecz': 'In the early 9th century, a small keep was built... Since 940 it was one of the key strongholds of the early Piast dynasty... in 1331, it was burnt to the ground, never [rebuilt/recovered].' Sacked once already in 1038 by Bretislaus I. A small village remains on the site.

name: Wiślica
why: Wikipedia 'Wiślica' gives no history, only that it 'was the smallest town in Poland in 2018.' Wiślica was the tribal capital of the Vistulans before the Piast unification of Poland and declined after Mongol raids of 1241 and 1259-60; this is from general knowledge, not the page (approx).

name: Otepää
why: Wikipedia 'Otepää': hill fort 'first mentioned in Rus' sources in 1116'; attacked in the Northern Crusades from 1208, 'finally conquered in 1224 by German crusaders'; 'importance of Otepää waned as Tartu... grew,' and 'it is more commonly believed that the castle was razed by the Livonian Order in 1396.'

name: Valjala
why: Wikipedia 'Valjala': chief stronghold of Saaremaa, with a 12th-century dry stone wall found in 2023-24 excavations. The Danish/German conquest of Saaremaa in 1227, which ended its independent role, is from general knowledge, not stated on the page (approx).

name: Tērvete
why: Wikipedia 'Tērvete': 'famous for the historic hillfort built for the kings of Western Semigallia (Zemgale) in the Middle Ages... In 1287, the Semigallian castle was destroyed by the Livonian Order.' A wooden Order castle built nearby in 1335 was itself destroyed by Lithuanian forces in 1345.

name: Jersika
why: Wikipedia 'Principality of Jersika': 'one of the largest medieval states in Latvia before the Northern Crusades,' with its capital on a hillfort 165 km southeast of Riga. The principality's end (1239, per general knowledge of the Northern Crusades) is not itself dated on the page (approx).

name: Veliky Novgorod
why: Wikipedia 'Veliky Novgorod': 'first mentioned in the 9th century... The Charter of Veliky Novgorod recognizes 859 as the year... it was first mentioned and therefore the year it was founded.' 'From 1136 to 1478, it was the center of... the Novgorod Republic,' annexed by Moscow in 1478.

name: Pskov
why: Wikipedia 'Pskov': 'Its earliest mention comes in 903'; became capital of the 'de facto sovereign' Pskov Republic in 1348; 'in 1510, the city was annexed by the Grand Duchy of Moscow.'

name: Smolensk
why: Wikipedia 'Smolensk': 'First mentioned in 863... beginning as the capital of the Principality of Smolensk.' 'The last sovereign monarch of Smolensk was Yury of Smolensk; during his reign the city was taken by Vytautas the Great of Lithuania... in 1395, 1404, and 1408,' ending its independence.

name: Chernihiv
why: Wikipedia 'Chernihiv': 'first mentioned... in the Rus'-Byzantine Treaty (907)... second most important city after Kyiv.' 'The golden age of Chernigov... lasted until 1239 when the city was sacked by the hordes of Batu Khan, and entered a long period of relative obscurity.'

name: Polotsk
why: Wikipedia 'Polotsk': 'The Primary Chronicle mentioned Polotsk in the year 862.' It 'repeatedly asserted its sovereignty' as capital of the Principality of Polotsk until 'the Grand Duke of Lithuania Vytenis annexed the city by military force in 1307.'

name: Vladimir
why: Wikipedia 'Vladimir, Russia': founding date 'disputed between 990 and 1108' (1108 the Soviet-era consensus, used here, approx); became capital of Vladimir-Suzdal under Andrey Bogolyubsky from 1157, with a 'Golden Age' that 'lasted until the Mongol invasion of Rus' in 1237,' the city 'finally overrun on February 8, 1238.'

name: Suzdal
why: Wikipedia 'Suzdal': 'first mentioned in chronicles under the year 1024'; capital of the Rostov-Suzdal principality until 1157, later capital of its own Principality of Suzdal (1238) and then Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal (1341-50); 'In 1392, Grand Prince Vasily I of Moscow annexed the principality.'

name: Rostov Veliky
why: Wikipedia 'Rostov Veliky': 'first mentioned in sources under the year 862 as an already important settlement... became the center of the Principality of Rostov... finally incorporated into the Grand Principality of Moscow in 1474.'

name: Turov
why: Wikipedia 'Turov, Belarus': 'ancient capital of the Dregovich tribe... first mentioned in the Tale of Bygone Years from 980'; 'one of the most important cities of the Rus among Kiev, Chernihiv, Novgorod, and Pereyaslav.' 'The town's period of prosperity ended with a number of feudal conflicts in the 12th century.'

name: Halych
why: Wikipedia 'Halych': in 1141 Prince Volodymyrko 'transferred his capital from Zvenyhorod to Halych,' which became capital of the Principality/Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia; 'The Mongols under Batu Khan took the capital in 1241... Thereafter the town steadily declined, eventually ceding supremacy to the newly founded Lviv.'

name: Zvenyhorod
why: Wikipedia 'Zvenyhorod': 'was the capital of the former Principality of Zvenyhorod (11th and 12th centuries).' Ceased to be capital in 1141 when Volodymyrko moved his seat to Halych (dated on the Halych page).

name: Volodymyr
why: Wikipedia 'Volodymyr, Ukraine': 'one of the oldest cities in Ukraine... served as the capital of the Principality of Volhynia and later as one of the capital cities of the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia.' Traditional founding by Vladimir the Great c. 988 (approx, not stated on the page); the Galicia-Volhynia kingdom's partition between Poland and Lithuania in the 1340s ended its capital status (approx).

name: Vyshhorod
why: Wikipedia 'Vyshhorod': 'First mentioned in the 10th century' (946 in general chronicle tradition, approx); a key Kievan Rus' fortress-town on the Dnieper. The Mongol invasion of the Kyiv region (1240) is the general marker used for the end of its medieval prominence (approx).

name: Pereiaslav
why: Wikipedia 'Pereiaslav': 'one of the key regional centers of power during the Middle Ages and served as the capital of a principality.' Traditional founding by Vladimir the Great c. 992 (approx, not on the page); decline dated by general reference to the 1239 Mongol invasion of the region (approx).

name: Vshchizh
why: Wikipedia 'Vshchizh': 'an old Russian town... first mentioned in a chronicle of 1142... In 1238, Vshchizh was destroyed by the Mongols. Later, Vshchizh was reborn as a village that exists to this day.'

name: Liubech
why: Wikipedia 'Liubech': 'First mentioned in 882, Liubech later became a town in the Principality of Chernigov.' Its decline as a significant town, like Chernihiv's, is placed at the mid-13th century Mongol invasion by general knowledge, not stated on the page (approx). A rural settlement of the same name continues today.

name: Korosten
why: Wikipedia 'Korosten': 'also historically known as Iskorosten,' capital of the Drevlians; the town's flag commemorates 'the bravery and courage of the Drevlian defenders of the city in 946 when Princess Olga laid siege to Korosten' -- she besieged and burned the city in revenge for the killing of her husband Igor. Founding as a Drevlian tribal centre is approximate.

name: Belgorod Kyivskyi
why: Wikipedia 'Bilhorod Kyivskyi': 'a city-castle in Kievan Rus'... Established in 991... it stood on the roadway connecting Kyiv with... Zhytomyr and Halych, but was destroyed by the Tatars.' No exact destruction year given; 1240 (fall of Kyiv) used as a general marker (approx). Its ruins lie near the present-day village of Bilohorodka.

name: Pereyaslavets
why: Wikipedia 'Pereyaslavets': 'a trade city located near mouths of the Danube... captured by Prince Svyatoslav of Kievan Rus in 968.' The city's location itself is disputed among several Bulgarian and Romanian sites. Its role ended with Svyatoslav's defeat and withdrawal from Bulgaria (971, general knowledge, approx).

name: Plisnesk
why: Wikipedia 'Plisnesk archaeological complex': early medieval settlement of up to 450 ha, 'a Polis-like city and one of the centers of early medieval tribe of Croats.' 'The city's downfall and layers of burning are considered to be related to the Vladimir the Great's war with the Croats (992-993).'

name: Chufut-Kale
why: Wikipedia 'Chufut-Kale': 'probably a fortified settlement in the 5th or 6th century... existed as early as the seventh century,' known as Kyrk-Or; conquered by the Golden Horde in 1299, later a Crimean Khan's residence; after the 1783 Russian annexation, 'Chufut-Kale was deserted. By the mid-19th century the town ceased to exist.'

name: Sudak
why: Wikipedia 'Sudak': 'local tradition places its foundation in 212 CE'; as Sougdaia it was a major Silk Road/Black Sea trade terminus, taken by the Genoese from Kaffa in 1365; 'Genoese rule lasted until 1475, when the Ottoman Grand Vizier Gedik Ahmed Pasha captured it.' A resort town continues on the site.

name: Eski-Kermen
why: Wikipedia 'Eski-Kermen': 'a cave town and fortress in the Crimea... Founded by the Byzantine Empire in the 6th century to defend against the Göktürks, it was conquered by the Khazars in the 7th or 8th century... it remained a thriving cave dwelling until at least the 11th century, during the rule of the Pechenegs. It seems to have been deserted in the 14th century, under the rule of the Tatars.'

name: Kaffa
why: Wikipedia 'Feodosia': 'During much of its history, the city was a significant settlement known as Caffa... or Kaffa.' The Genoese colony's traditional founding year (1266, general knowledge, approx) is not stated on the page; it fell to the Ottomans in 1475 (dated on the Mangup page for the same campaign). The ancient Greek colony of Theodosia on the same site is Pleiades territory; modern Feodosia continues today.

name: Old Ryazan
why: Wikipedia 'Ryazan': 'An older city, now known as Old Ryazan... was located 50 km east of modern-day Ryazan during the late Middle Ages, and served as capital of the Principality of Ryazan up until the Mongol invasion in 1237. During the Siege of Ryazan, it became one of the first cities in Russia to be besieged and completely razed to the ground.' First chronicle mention (1095) is from general knowledge (approx); a new capital, Pereyaslavl-Ryazansky, was founded elsewhere and later renamed Ryazan.

name: Reric
why: Wikipedia 'Reric': 'one of the Viking Age multi-ethnic Slavic-Scandinavian emporia on the southern coast of the Baltic Sea... established probably in 735... It was destroyed in 808 AD by the Viking (Danish) king Gudfred... rebuilt by the Obodrites and continued to operate for a short [time] until Drasco was murdered in Reric in 810.' Its merchants were then moved to Hedeby.

name: Liubice
why: Wikipedia 'Liubice': 'also known by the German name Alt-Lübeck ("Old Lübeck"), was a medieval West Slavic settlement near the site of modern Lübeck... the residence of Henry, the Christian prince of the Obotrites, Liubice was destroyed after his death by the Rani pagans of Rugia.' Henry died in 1127; general knowledge places the destruction at 1138 (approx). Modern Lübeck, founded nearby in 1143, is a separate site and not this entry.

name: Starigard
why: Wikipedia 'Oldenburg in Holstein': chief town of the Slavic Wagrians/Obotrites, who 'arrived about A.D. 700'; the Slavic name Starigard/Stargard meant 'Old Settlement.' Emperor Otto I established the bishopric of Oldenburg there. A German town of the same (translated) name continues today; the Slavic-era bishopric's end (transferred to Lübeck in 1163, general knowledge) marks the end of Starigard's own heyday (approx).

name: Jaromarsburg
why: Wikipedia 'Jaromarsburg': 'a cult site for the Slavic tribe of Rani dedicated to the god Svantovit and used from the 9th to the 12th century,' at Cape Arkona on Rügen, 'protected on two sides by the cliffed coast and from the land side by a Slavic burgwall.' The Rani stronghold and temple of Arkona were destroyed by the Danish king Valdemar I in 1168 (general knowledge, approx).

name: Rungholt
why: Wikipedia 'Rungholt': 'a low-lying settlement in North Frisia... Rungholt was flooded, with massive erosion, when a storm tide (known as Grote Mandrenke... ) hit the coast on 15 or 16 January 1362.' Founding date not given on the page; c. 1200 is a general estimate (approx for 'from' only).

name: Ny Varberg
why: Wikipedia 'Ny Varberg': 'a city founded sometime between 1429 and 1434 about five kilometres north of present-day Varberg, Sweden... It was abandoned around 1612.'

name: Pustozersk
why: Wikipedia 'Pustozersk': 'the first town built by Russians north of the Arctic Circle... founded in 1499 in the lower reaches of the Pechora River by Princes Semyon Kurbsky and Pyotr Ushaty.' The town was eventually abandoned in the Soviet period.

name: Dobrzyń nad Wisłą
why: Wikipedia 'Dobrzyń nad Wisłą' gives only its modern description (a small town of about 2,000). It was the medieval seat of the Dobrzyń Land and the Order of Dobrzyń (a short-lived crusading order founded here in 1228); an 11th-century founding is from general knowledge, not the page (approx). Continues today as a small town, much reduced from its medieval standing as a land/castellany seat.

name: Brenna
