why: Wikipedia 'Brandenburg an der Havel': 'served as the capital of the Margraviate of Brandenburg until it was replaced by Berlin in 1417... Today, it is a small town compared to nearby Berlin.' The Slavic Hevelli stronghold on the site (Brenna/Brandenburg), taken by German King Henry I in 929, is from general knowledge, not stated on the page (approx). Entry covers the Slavic-era stronghold rather than the later medieval margravial capital.

name: Sigtuna
why: Wikipedia 'Sigtuna': 'Present-day Sigtuna, a harbour town that was established around 980,' succeeding Birka as Sweden's leading trading town. Its raiding/destruction of 1187 (traditionally by Curonians or Estonians, after which Stockholm eventually eclipsed it) is from general knowledge, not stated on the page (approx). A small town of about 9,700 continues on the site.

name: Ryurikovo Gorodishche
why: Wikipedia 'Ryurikovo Gorodishche': 'the primary settlement in the area known in Scandinavian sources as Holmgård. Founded in the 9th century, it was the predecessor of the modern site of Veliky Novgorod,' 2 km south of the current city centre. By 930 the elite residences had merged into the new site of Novgorod itself (dated on the Veliky Novgorod page).

name: Izyaslavl
why: Wikipedia 'Zaslawye' gives only the modern description of the Belarusian town (population 17,116); it does not cover its early history. By general knowledge, the town was founded c. 985 by Vladimir the Great as Izyaslavl, for his wife Rogneda and their son Izyaslav, after his conquest of Polotsk; not stated on the page (approx).

name: Peresopnytsia
why: Wikipedia 'Peresopnytsia': 'In 11th-13th centuries it was one of two main cities of Horyn River basin. In the 12th century Peresopnytsia was a capital of the Peresopnytsia principality... a regional principality of the Principality of Volhynia.' No explicit decline date given; c. 1200 (absorption into Volhynia) is a general estimate (approx). Now a small village, later famous for the 1561 Peresopnytsia Gospel.

name: Lothal
why: Wikipedia 'Lothal': 'Construction of the city is believed to have begun around 2300 BCE'; Indus Valley sites were largely abandoned by c. 1900 BCE as the civilisation declined (approximate).

name: Rakhigarhi
why: Wikipedia 'Rakhigarhi': belonged to 'the pre-Harappan (6000?/4600-3300 BC), early Harappan (3300-2600 BC), and the mature phase (2600-1900 BC) of the Indus Valley Civilisation'; abandoned at the end of the mature phase (approximate).

name: Kalibangan
why: Wikipedia 'Kalibangan': 'It is around 2900 BC that the region of Kalibangan developed into' a major provincial capital of the Indus Valley Civilization; the town was abandoned with the wider IVC decline c. 1900 BCE (approximate).

name: Ganeriwala
why: Wikipedia 'Ganweriwal': 'one of the largest cities within the Indus Valley civilisation... believed to have been a city centre within the civilization'; dated to the mature Harappan phase, ending c. 1900 BCE (approximate).

name: Banawali
why: Wikipedia 'Banawali': Period I Pre-Harappan c. 2500-2300 BCE through Period III Post-Harappan (Banawali-Bara) c. 1700-1500/1450 BCE, after which the site was abandoned.

name: Kot Diji
why: Wikipedia 'Kot Diji': 'an ancient site... estimated to have been occupied around 3300 BCE', part of the early/formative Indus civilisation; occupation ended with the wider IVC decline c. 1900 BCE (approximate).

name: Chanhudaro
why: Wikipedia 'Chanhudaro': 'The settlement was inhabited between 4000 and 1700 BCE, and is considered to have been a centre for manufacturing carnelian beads.'

name: Surkotada
why: Wikipedia 'Surkotada': 'a smaller fortified IVC site'; dated to the mature-to-late Harappan phase (approximate, general IVC chronology).

name: Amri
why: Wikipedia 'Amri, Sindh': 'goes back to 3600 BCE'; 'the earliest phase was a fortified town that flourished from 3600 to 3300 BC'; the wider Amri culture continued into contact with the Harappan phase before decline (approximate end).

name: Nausharo
why: Wikipedia 'Nausharo': 'occupied between 3000 and 2550 BC and again between 2550 and 1900 BC.'

name: Sutkagan Dor
why: Wikipedia 'Sutkagan Dor': 'the westernmost known archaeological site of the Indus Valley civilisation... a smaller settlement with substantial stone walls and gateways', dated to the general Harappan mature phase ending c. 1900 BCE (approximate).

name: Ayodhya
why: Wikipedia 'Ayodhya': 'The settlement was historically known as Saketa until it was renamed to Ayodhya during the Gupta period'; continues today as a city (approximate founding date, general knowledge of Ganges-valley Iron Age settlement).

name: Mathura
why: Wikipedia 'Mathura': 'Mathura was the capital of the kingdom of Surasena, ruled by Kamsa'; 'an economic hub, located at the junction of important caravan routes' in ancient times; continues today as a city (approximate founding, Mahajanapada period).

name: Kaushambi
why: Wikipedia 'Kaushambi' (redirect to Kosambi): an ancient city of India, capital of the Vatsa kingdom; the site continues today as the village of Kosam near Prayagraj (approximate dates, general knowledge of Vatsa Mahajanapada chronology).

name: Shravasti
why: Wikipedia 'Shravasti': 'the capital of the ancient Indian kingdom of Kosala, where the Buddha lived most after his enlightenment'; continues today as a town (approximate founding date, Mahajanapada period).

name: Vaishali
why: Wikipedia 'Vaishali (ancient city)': 'the capital city of the Vajjika League... dates from c. 6th century BCE'; the city declined after the Gupta period (approximate end, general knowledge).

name: Rajagriha
why: Wikipedia 'Rajgir': 'the first capital of the ancient kingdom of Magadha'; 'ceramics dating to about 1000 BCE have been found'; continues today as the town of Rajgir.

name: Hastinapura
why: Wikipedia 'Hastinapur': 'described as the capital of the Kuru kingdom in Hindu texts such as the Mahabharata'; continues today as a town in Meerut district (approximate founding, Painted Grey Ware / Kuru-period chronology).

name: Kapilavastu
why: Wikipedia 'Kapilavastu': ancient city of the Indian subcontinent, capital of the Shakyas (Buddha's home city); proposed sites Piprahwa (India) and Tilaurakot (Nepal) are villages today, so the ancient capital is treated as abandoned under this name (approximate dates, Mahajanapada period).

name: Kushinagar
why: Wikipedia 'Kushinagar': the town where 'Gautama Buddha is believed to have attained parinirvana'; continues today as a town (approximate founding).

name: Takshashila
why: Wikipedia 'Taxila': 'Founded around c. 1000 BC... one of the capitals of the Gandhara civilisation'; the ancient city was sacked by the Huns c. 5th century and later abandoned, though a modern town of the same-derived name continues nearby (approximate).

name: Pushkalavati
why: Wikipedia 'Pushkalavati': 'capital of the ancient region of Gandhara'; 'remained an important city... through to the beginning of the 3rd century CE'; the site is now the modern town of Charsadda.

name: Ujjain
why: Wikipedia 'Ujjain': 'then known as Avantika, it was the most prominent city on the Malwa plateau... from the time of the ancient Mahajanapadas'; continues today as a city (approximate founding).

name: Vidisha
why: Wikipedia 'Vidisha': 'formerly known as Bhelsa, Besnagar and Bhaddalpur in ancient times... renamed Vidisha in 1956'; continues today as a city (approximate founding).

name: Ahichhatra
why: Wikipedia 'Ahichchhatra': 'the ancient capital of Northern Panchala'; excavations 'uncovered nine strata, the lowest from before the 3rd century BCE and the latest from the 11th century CE', after which the site was abandoned.

name: Sisupalgarh
why: Wikipedia 'Sisupalgarh': 'First inhabited around 7th to 6th centuries BCE... once the capital of ancient Kalinga'; B.B. Lal dated the fort city to flourishing 'between 3rd century BC and 4th century AD', after which it was abandoned.

name: Bairat
why: Wikipedia 'Viratnagar': the site 'corresponds to the ancient city of Viratanagara, which was the capital of the Iron Age Matsya kingdom (c. 1400-c. 350 BC)'; continues today as the town of Viratnagar.

name: Mahasthangarh
why: Wikipedia 'Mahasthangarh': 'dates Mahasthangarh to at least the 3rd century BCE... an important city under the Maurya Empire. The fortified area of the city was in use until the 8th century CE'; the village of Mahasthan continues on the site today.

name: Wari-Bateshwar
why: Wikipedia 'Wari-Bateshwar ruins': 'primarily occupied during the Iron Age, from 400 to 100 BCE'; one of the oldest urban archaeological sites in Bangladesh, since abandoned.

name: Balkh
why: Wikipedia 'Balkh': known to the Greeks as Bactra, 'renowned as the capital of Bactria and later Tokharistan'; 'suffered severely due to the Mongol invasion in the 13th century and never recovered its former status'; a city of 148,972 continues today.

name: Ghazni
why: Wikipedia 'Ghazni': 'anciently known as Alexandria in Opiana'; capital of the medieval Ghaznavid Empire; continues today as a provincial capital of about 206,000 people (approximate ancient founding).

name: Bamiyan
why: Wikipedia 'Bamyan': historic hub of Buddhism on the Silk Road (site of the Bamiyan Buddhas); continues today as the capital of Bamyan Province (approximate ancient founding, general knowledge).

name: Kapisi
why: Wikipedia 'Bagram': 'The ancient city of Kapisi is identified with present-day Bagram... Bagram was the capital of the Kushan Empire in the first century [AD]'; the modern town of Bagram continues on the site.

name: Hund
why: Wikipedia 'Hund, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa': 'known in antiquity as Udabhandapura'; 'the last capital of Gandhara... under the Hindu Shahi rulers until the beginning of 11th century AD, when Mahmud of Ghazni defeated Anandapala'; a small village continues on the site today.

name: Banbhore
why: Wikipedia 'Banbhore': 'a city dating to the 1st century BCE'; 'controlled by Muslims from the 8th to the 13th century, after which it was abandoned.'

name: Brahmanabad
why: Wikipedia 'Mansura, Sindh': 'the historic capital of the caliphal province of Sindh... from the year 750 AD to 1006 AD', built over the earlier city of Brahmanabad; declined after the Ghaznavid conquest of Sindh in the early 11th century (approximate end).

name: Aror
why: Wikipedia 'Aror': 'once served as the capital of Sindh'; 'In 962 it was hit by a massive earthquake that changed the course of the Indus River and ruined the town's mud brick buildings... setting into play the city's decline, and eventual re-settlement at Rohri.'

name: Thatta
why: Wikipedia 'Thatta': 'the medieval capital of Sindh... Its construction was ordered by Jam Nizamuddin II in 1495'; continues today as a city.

name: Uch
why: Wikipedia 'Uch': 'may have been founded as Alexandria on the Indus'; 'a regional metropolitan centre between the 12th and 17th centuries'; continues today as a small city (approximate founding).

name: Parihaspora
why: Wikipedia 'Parihaspore': 'built by Lalitaditya Muktapida (695-731 CE) and served as the capital of Kashmir during his reign'; declined after his reign ended (approximate).

name: Avantipura
why: Wikipedia 'Awantipora': 'founded by Avantivarman the Kashmiri Hindu ruler, who was the first king of the Utpala dynasty and ruled Kashmir from 855 to 883 AD'; continues today as a town.

name: Bhinmal
why: Wikipedia 'Bhinmal': 'the early capital of Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty'; visited by Xuanzang 631-645 AD; continues today as a town (approximate founding).

name: Prabhas Patan
why: Wikipedia 'Somnath Temple': ancient pilgrimage port town at 'Prabhas Patan, Veraval, in Gujarat'; 'various texts... mention a tirtha (pilgrimage site) at Prabhas Patan on the coastline of Saurashtra'; the town continues today (approximate ancient dating).

name: Bharuch
why: Wikipedia 'Bharuch': 'settled since times of antiquity... a ship building centre and sea port'; 'known to the Greeks, the Parthian Empire, the Romans, the Chinese'; continues today as a city (approximate ancient founding).

name: Junagadh
why: Wikipedia 'Junagadh': 'referred to by names such as Girivraja and Ujjayanta, reflecting its antiquity'; continues today as a city (approximate ancient founding).

name: Anahilapataka
why: Wikipedia 'Patan, Gujarat': 'established by the Chavda ruler Vanaraja in the ninth century as "Anahilapataka"'; 'capital of Gujarat's Chavda and Chaulukya dynasties'; continues today as a city.

name: Champaner
why: Wikipedia 'Champaner': 'founded by Vanraj Chavda... in the 8th century'; 'briefly the capital of the Sultanate of Gujarat' after Mahmud Begada's conquest in 1484; the Mughal-Gujarat wars of the 1530s ended its importance, though a small town continues on the site.

name: Dwarka
why: Wikipedia 'Dwarka': 'a coastal town... one of the seven most ancient religious cities (Sapta Puri) in India'; traditionally associated with Krishna; continues today as a town (dating approximate and partly legendary/archaeologically debated).

name: Chittorgarh
why: Wikipedia 'Chittorgarh': 'a major stronghold of the Rajput State of Medapata (modern Mewar)'; 'sacked thrice; first in 1303... again in 1535... and lastly by the Mughal Emperor Akbar in 1568', after which Mewar's capital moved to Udaipur; a substantial city continues on the site.

name: Dhar
why: Wikipedia 'Dhar': capital of the Paramara dynasty and later of the Malwa Sultanate before the capital moved to Mandu; 'the capital of the Dhar princely state'; continues today as a city (approximate founding).

name: Chanderi
why: Wikipedia 'Chanderi': 'mentioned by the Persian scholar Alberuni in 1030'; captured for the Delhi Sultanate in 1251, later held by the Malwa Sultanate and Bundela Rajputs; a town of 33,190 continues today.

name: Bikaner
why: Wikipedia 'Bikaner': 'founded in 1488 CE by Rao Bika, a Rajput chief of the Rathore dynasty'; continues today as the fourth-largest city in Rajasthan.

name: Jaisalmer
why: Wikipedia 'Jaisalmer': 'a former medieval trading center and the historic capital of the kingdom of Jaisalmer, founded in 1156 by Rawal Jaisal'; continues today as a city.

name: Mandore
why: Wikipedia 'Mandore': seat of the Pratiharas of Mandavyapura from the 6th century CE; 'the Fort served as his family's capital until 1459 CE, when Rao Jodha shifted it to the newly-founded city of Jodhpur'; a suburb continues on the site.

name: Amber
why: Wikipedia 'Amber, India': conquered and made capital of Dhundhar 'around 1207 CE... Amber would remain the seat of the Kachwaha Rajput dynasty for the next 500 years' until Jaipur was founded in 1727; a town continues on the site.

name: Ahar
why: Wikipedia 'Ahar, Rajasthan': 'became the capital of the Guhil rulers of Mewar in c.948 and stayed so until c.1116 when the capital moved to Nagda'; now within the city of Udaipur.

name: Nagda
why: Wikipedia 'Nagda, Rajasthan': 'the first capital of Mewar'; 'again became the capital of Mewar and stayed so until the early part of the 13th century when it was sacked by Sultan Iltutmish's forces'; a village of population 237 continues today.

name: Vijayanagara
why: Wikipedia 'Hampi': 'the capital of the Vijayanagara (Karnata) Empire from 1336 to 1565... when it was abandoned'; the tourist village of Hampi continues on the site.

name: Warangal
why: Wikipedia 'Warangal': 'served as the capital of the Kakatiya dynasty which was established in 1163'; continues today as a city of over 800,000.

name: Bidar
why: Wikipedia 'Bidar': capital of the Bahmani Sultanate from 1427 and later of the Barid Shahi dynasty; 'the Bidar fort... is more than 500 years old'; continues today as a city.

name: Gulbarga
why: Wikipedia 'Kalaburagi': first capital of the Bahmani Sultanate, founded 1347, until the capital moved to Bidar in 1427; continues today as the city of Kalaburagi.

name: Bijapur
why: Wikipedia 'Bijapur': 'established in the 10th-11th centuries... known as Vijayapura'; conquered by the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347 and later capital of the Bijapur Sultanate; continues today as a city.

name: Golconda
why: Wikipedia 'Golconda': 'built by Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra in the 11th century'; 'made it the capital of the Sultanate of Golconda'; the Qutb Shahi capital moved to nearby Hyderabad in 1591 and the fortress fell to the Mughals in 1687, after which it declined to a ruin on Hyderabad's outskirts.

name: Devagiri
why: Wikipedia 'Daulatabad Fort': 'the capital of the Yadavas (9th century - 14th century CE), for a brief time the capital of the Delhi Sultanate (1327-1334), and later a secondary capital of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate (1499-1636)'; renamed Daulatabad in 1327; a village continues on the site.

name: Chandragiri
why: Wikipedia 'Chandragiri Fort, Andhra Pradesh': 'Chandragiri was the 4th capital of Vijayanagara Empire' after Penukonda fell to Golconda (approximate 1592-1646); a village continues on the site.

name: Penukonda
why: Wikipedia 'Penukonda': controlled by 'the Hoysalas, Chalukyas, Vijayanagar... and eventually came under British rule'; the third Vijayanagara capital after the fall of Hampi in 1565, until the capital moved to Chandragiri (approximate); continues today as a town.

name: Kanchipuram
why: Wikipedia 'Kanchipuram': 'known as the City of Thousand Temples'; a Pallava, and later Chola and Vijayanagara, capital; continues today as a city (approximate ancient founding).

name: Thanjavur
why: Wikipedia 'Thanjavur': capital of the Chola Empire, home to the Brihadisvara Temple 'built by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I'; continues today as a city (approximate Chola-era founding).

name: Gangaikonda Cholapuram
why: Wikipedia 'Gangaikonda Cholapuram': 'The Chola emperor Rajendra I established it as the capital of the Chola dynasty in c. 1025, and it remained the capital for approximately 250 years'; a heritage village continues on the site.

name: Vatapi
why: Wikipedia 'Badami': 'the regal capital of the Badami Chalukyas from 540 to 757'; continues today as the town of Badami.

name: Kalyani
why: Wikipedia 'Basavakalyan': 'the capital of the Kalyani Chalukyas and the Kalachuris of Kalyani'; renamed Basavakalyan in 1956 after India's independence; continues today as a city.

name: Srirangapatna
why: Wikipedia 'Srirangapatna': 'has since time immemorial been an urban center'; during the Vijayanagara Empire 'it became the seat of a major viceroyalty', later capital of the Kingdom of Mysore; continues today as a town.

name: Ahmednagar
why: Wikipedia 'Ahmednagar': capital of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate, home to 'several dozen buildings and sites from the Nizam Shahi period'; continues today as a city (officially renamed Ahilyanagar).

name: Burhanpur
why: Wikipedia 'Burhanpur': 'In 1388, Malik Nasir Khan, the Faruqi dynasty Sultan of Khandesh, discovered Burhanpur... Burhanpur became the capital of the Khandesh sultanate'; continues today as a city.

name: Achalpur
why: Wikipedia 'Achalpur': 'the earliest capital of a branch of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, which emerged sometime in the 8th century'; later capital of the Imad Shahi dynasty of Berar (1490); continues today as a city.

name: Cuttack
why: Wikipedia 'Cuttack': 'the former capital of the Indian state of Odisha'; the name derives from Kataka, 'a reference to the ancient Barabati Fort'; 'known as the Millennium City... due to its history of 1000 years'; continues today as Odisha's second-largest city (approximate founding).

name: Dharanikota
why: Wikipedia 'Dharanikota': site of ancient Dhanyakataka, 'the capital of the Satavahana dynasty... between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE'; 'also the capital of the Kota Vamsa, which ruled during the medieval period until the mid-12th century'; a village continues on the site.

name: Anuradhapura
why: Wikipedia 'Anuradhapura': 'the Mahavamsa places the founding of the city in 437 BCE... one of the oldest continuously occupied cities in Asia'; ceased to be the capital after the Chola invasion of 993; a city continues on the site today.

name: Polonnaruwa
why: Wikipedia 'Polonnaruwa': 'renamed Jananathamangalam by the Chola dynasty after their successful invasion of the country's then capital, Anuradhapura, in the 10th century'; the medieval kingdom's capital until the mid-13th century; a modern town continues on the site.

name: Sigiriya
why: Wikipedia 'Sigiriya': 'selected by King Kashyapa (CE 477-495) for his new capital'; 'the capital and the royal palace were abandoned after' Kashyapa's death in 495; a small town continues near the rock today.

name: Kandy
why: Wikipedia 'Kandy': 'the last capital of the Sinhalese monarchy from 1469 to 1818, under the Kingdom of Kandy'; continues today as a major city.

name: Dambadeniya
why: Wikipedia 'Dambadeniya': 'selected as the capital of the kingdom of Sri Lanka by King Vijayabahu III (1232-36)'; superseded when King Bhuvenakabahu moved the capital to Yapahuwa in 1272; the site continues as a small town.

name: Yapahuwa
why: Wikipedia 'Yapahuwa': 'In 1272, King Bhuvenakabahu transferred the capital from Dambadeniya to Yapahuwa'; 'following the death of King Bhuvenakabahu in 1284... Yapahuwa was largely abandoned and inhabited by Buddhist monks.'

name: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte
why: Wikipedia 'Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte': capital of the Kingdom of Kotte in medieval Sri Lanka; today 'the legislative capital city of Sri Lanka' (approximate founding date, general knowledge of the Kotte kingdom).

name: Jaffna
why: Wikipedia 'Jaffna': suburb 'Nallur served as the capital of the four-century-long medieval Tamil Jaffna Kingdom'; continues today as a city (approximate founding of the kingdom).

name: Lalitpur
why: Wikipedia 'Lalitpur, Nepal': locally called Yala, one of the three kingdoms of the Kathmandu Valley; 'chronicles like the Gopal Raj Vamshavali put the foundation of Bhaktapur in the 12th century' and Patan (Lalitpur) is traditionally dated earlier still; continues today as a metropolitan city (approximate founding).

name: Bhaktapur
why: Wikipedia 'Bhaktapur': historically called Bhadgaon; 'chronicles... put the foundation of Bhaktapur in the 12th century'; one of the three kingdoms of the Kathmandu Valley; continues today as a city.

name: Sonargaon
why: Wikipedia 'Sonargaon': 'one of the old capitals of the historic region of Bengal'; 'gained importance during the Delhi Sultanate... was the capital of the Sonargaon Sultanate'; superseded as capital by Dhaka in the early 17th century; a town continues on the site.

name: Gaur
why: Wikipedia 'Gauda (city)': 'Gauda was the fifth-most populous city in' the world in 1500, per Eaton; 'For a period of 112 years, between 1453 and 1565, Gauda was the capital of the Bengal Sultanate'; a village continues on the site today.

name: Pandua
why: Wikipedia 'Pandua, Malda': 'the first capital city of the Bengal Sultanate for 114 years (1339-1453)... the capital later shifted to Gaur'; 'now almost synonymously known as Adina, a small town.'

name: Panam Nagar
why: Wikipedia 'Panam Nagar': traces its origins to the 13th century; 'declined in the 17th century following the relocation of the capital from Sonargaon'; revived by merchants in the 19th century, but 'the partition of India and riots in 1964 led to its abandonment.'

name: Bagan
why: Wikipedia 'Bagan': 'the capital of the Pagan Kingdom, the first kingdom that unified the regions that would later constitute Myanmar', from the 9th to 13th centuries; a UNESCO-listed town continues on the site.

name: Sri Ksetra
why: Wikipedia 'Sri Ksetra kingdom': 'the largest' Pyu settlement, 'the largest Southeast Asian city before Angkor times'; 'material is dated between the seventh and ninth centuries AD'; the site is now uninhabited near modern Hmawza.

name: Beikthano
why: Wikipedia 'Beikthano': 'a city of considerable significance, possibly a local capital replacing Sri Ksetra'; part of the Pyu city-states heritage 'traced back... to between 200 BC and 900 AD'; now an uninhabited archaeological zone (approximate).

name: Halin
why: Wikipedia 'Hanlin, Burma': 'a city of considerable significance, possibly a local capital replacing Sri Ksetra'; the archaeological sites lie above the modern village (approximate Pyu-era dates).

name: Mrauk U
why: Wikipedia 'Mrauk U': 'From 1430 until 1785, it was the capital of the Mrauk U Kingdom, the largest and most powerful Rakhine kingdom in history'; a town continues on the site.

name: Ava
why: Wikipedia 'Inwa': 'an ancient imperial capital of successive Burmese kingdoms from the 14th to 19th centuries... finally abandoned after it was destroyed by a series of major earthquakes in March 1839.'

name: Pinya
why: Wikipedia 'Pinya kingdom': 'the kingdom that ruled Central Myanmar (Burma) from 1313 to 1365', founded as successor state to Pagan; its capital was later abandoned when Ava was founded (approximate coordinates, near Ava).

name: Sagaing
why: Wikipedia 'Sagaing': classical name Jeyyapura; capital of an independent kingdom from 1315-17; 'today, with about 70,000 inhabitants, the city is part of Mandalay metropolitan area.'

name: Taungoo
why: Wikipedia 'Taungoo': 'founded in 1279 in the waning days of Pagan'; 'in the 16th century it was the first capital of the Toungoo dynasty'; continues today as a city.

name: Hanthawaddy
why: Wikipedia 'Bago, Myanmar': 'formerly known as Hanthawaddy... a historical capital of the Taungoo Dynasty'; renamed Bago (from Pegu) in 1989; continues today as a city (approximate founding of the Hanthawaddy kingdom).

name: Martaban
why: Wikipedia 'Mottama': 'formerly Martaban... was the capital of the Martaban Kingdom (later known as Hanthawaddy Kingdom) from 1287 to 1364, and an entrepot of international repute until the mid-16th century.'

name: Thaton
why: Wikipedia 'Thaton kingdom': 'a Mon kingdom, believed to have existed in Lower Burma from at least the 4th century BC to the middle of the 11th century AD'; 'it was the Pagan kingdom from the north that conquered' Thaton in 1057; a town continues on the site.

name: Prome
why: Wikipedia 'Pyay': 'formerly anglicised as Prome'; an important trade centre on the Irrawaddy; renamed Pyay in 1989; continues today as a town (approximate medieval founding as a Pyu-successor centre).

name: Amarapura
why: Wikipedia 'Amarapura': 'founded by King Bodawpaya... as his new capital in May 1783'; 'finally being supplanted by Mandalay 11 kilometres north in 1859'; now a township of Mandalay.

name: Sukhothai
why: Wikipedia 'Sukhothai Historical Park': covers 'the ruins of Sukhothai... capital of the Sukhothai Kingdom in the 13th and 14th centuries'; the kingdom was absorbed into Ayutthaya by 1438 (approximate); the modern town of Sukhothai Thani lies nearby.

name: Ayutthaya
why: Wikipedia 'Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya (city)': 'the capital of the Ayutthaya Kingdom and, between the 14th and 18th centuries, grew into one of the world's largest cities... before its destruction during the Burmese invasion of 1767'; the city continues today as a smaller provincial capital.

name: Lopburi
why: Wikipedia 'Lopburi': 'one of the larger moated settlements of the Dvaravati period'; 'As Lavapura, or Lavo, it was incorporated into the Khmer Empire under Suryavarman I'; continues today as a city (approximate Dvaravati-era founding).

name: Nakhon Pathom
why: Wikipedia 'Nakhon Pathom': 'often said to have stood on the Gulf of Thailand two thousand years ago'; a leading centre of the Dvaravati culture; continues today as a city (approximate ancient founding).

name: U Thong
why: Wikipedia 'U Thong district': 'occupied for many centuries before the Dvaravati state developed'; radiocarbon work places 'the transition to complex state societies in the Chao Phraya basin between about 300 and 600 AD'; a district town continues on the site.

name: Si Thep
why: Wikipedia 'Si Thep' (Historical Park): an ancient city site of the Dvaravati and Khmer periods in what is now an archaeological park (approximate dates, general knowledge of the Si Thep site's chronology).

name: Chiang Saen
why: Wikipedia 'Chiang Saen': chronicles describe 'an ancient royal city, Ngoenyang, which was probably the first major city in the area'; continues today as a town on the Mekong (approximate founding of Ngoenyang/Chiang Saen).

name: Chiang Mai
why: Wikipedia 'Chiang Mai': capital of the Lanna kingdom, meaning 'new city'; 'bordered by ancient red brick walls... and has a moat surrounding it'; continues today as the largest city in northern Thailand.

name: Kamphaeng Phet
why: Wikipedia 'Kamphaeng Phet': 'in 1156 a monarch of Xian... moved his royal seat to Vicitraprakara, identified with present-day Kamphaeng Phet'; later 'a frontier stronghold' of Sukhothai; continues today as a town.

name: Phimai
why: Wikipedia 'Phimai': 'the region was integrated into the Khmer Empire around 1000 CE. For the following 300 years, Phimai was a major regional administrative center'; a township continues on the site.

name: Luang Prabang
why: Wikipedia 'Luang Prabang': historically known as Xieng Thong; capital of Lan Xang and later of Laos's royal family until 1975; continues today as a UNESCO-listed city (approximate early founding).

name: Champasak
why: Wikipedia 'Champasak (town)': 'once the seat of the Kingdom of Champasak, an independent Lao state that was abolished by the French in 1945'; 'today the town is very small', continuing on the site.

name: Hariharalaya
why: Wikipedia 'Hariharalaya': 'an ancient city and capital of the Khmer empire located near Siem Reap... in an area now called Roluos'; 'today, all that remains of the city are the ruins of several royal temples' (approximate dates, general knowledge of the pre-Angkorian to early Angkorian transition).

name: Koh Ker
why: Wikipedia 'Koh Ker': known in inscriptions as Lingapura or Chok Gargyar; 'under the reign of the kings Jayavarman IV and Harshavarman II Koh Ker was briefly the capital of the whole empire (928-944 AD).'

name: Isanapura
why: Wikipedia 'Sambor Prei Kuk': 'the now ruined complex dates back to the Pre-Angkorian Chenla Kingdom (late 6th to 9th century), established by king Isanavarman I as central royal sanctuary and capital, known then as Isanapura' (approximate span).

name: Angkor Borei
why: Wikipedia 'Angkor Borei District': 'this city was a settlement of the Kingdom of Funan and may have been its capital'; excavation focused on 'sociopolitical complexity from 500 BC to 500 AD'; a district town of the same name continues today (approximate Funan-era dates).

name: Longvek
why: Wikipedia 'Longvek': 'the second capital city during... Cambodia's post-Angkor period'; 'Ang Chan I... moved the capital city from Chaktomuk to Longvek in 1529'; sacked by Siam in 1594.

name: Oudong
why: Wikipedia 'Oudong': 'a former town of the post-Angkorian period (1618-1863)... Cambodia's capital for almost 250 years until 1866'; a town continues on the site.

name: Co Loa
why: Wikipedia 'Citadel of Co Loa': 'closely associated with An Duong Vuong, the king of Au Lac... might be the first political center of the Vietnamese civilization'; a modern district of Hanoi continues on the site (approximate founding).

name: Hoa Lu
why: Wikipedia 'Hoa Lu' (Ancient Capital): capital of Dai Viet under the Dinh and early Le dynasties before the capital moved to Thang Long (Hanoi) in 1010; a ward of Ninh Binh continues on the site.

name: Tay Do
why: Wikipedia 'Citadel of the Ho Dynasty': 'served as the western capital of the Ho dynasty (1398-1407) while also being an important political, economic, and cultural centre in the 16th to the 18th century'; now a stone fortress ruin.

name: Simhapura
why: Wikipedia 'Tra Kieu': 'the first capital city of the Hindu Champa Kingdom, then named Simhapura, from the 4th century to the 8th century CE'; a village continues on the site.

name: Indrapura
why: Wikipedia 'Indrapura (Champa)': 'the capital city of the kingdom of Champa from 875 AD until 982, or until 12th century AD... built and ruled under the reign of Buddhist king Indravarman II'; the modern toponym Dong Duong continues on the site.

name: Vijaya
why: Wikipedia 'Vijaya (Champa)': 'served as the capital of the Kingdom of Champa from 938 until it was conquered by Dai Viet during the Champa-Dai Viet War of 1471'; located in modern An Nhon, which continues on the site.

name: Panduranga
why: Wikipedia 'Panduranga (Champa)': 'the rump state of the Champa kingdom after... Le Thanh Tong destroyed Champa in 1471'; 'stood until late 17th century when the Nguyen lords... vassalized it'; its centre continues as modern Phan Rang.

name: Oc Eo
why: Wikipedia 'Oc Eo': 'a busy port of the kingdom of Funan between the 2nd century BC and 12th century AD... may have been the port known to the Greeks and Romans as Cattigara'; a modern commune of the same name continues on the site.

name: Trowulan
why: Wikipedia 'Trowulan': theorised site of the Majapahit Empire's capital, 'known as Majapahit or Wilwatikta'; 'razed during the invasion of Girindrawardhana to defeat Kertabhumi in 1478'; a modern subdistrict continues on the site.

name: Muaro Jambi
why: Wikipedia 'Muaro Jambi': archaeological site of Buddhist temple compounds associated with the Melayu Kingdom and Srivijaya-era trade on the Batang Hari river; a modern village and regency of the same name continue on the site (approximate dates, general knowledge of Melayu Kingdom chronology).

name: Kartasura
why: Wikipedia 'Kartasura': 'in the seventeenth century Kartasura was the capital of the Sultanate of Mataram between 1680 and 1755'; 'preceded the transfer to Surakarta by Pakubuwana II'; a district continues on the site.

name: Demak
why: Wikipedia 'Demak': capital of the sixteenth-century Demak Sultanate, the first major Islamic state on Java; continues today as a large town on Java's north coast (approximate founding).

name: Banten
why: Wikipedia 'Banten (town)': capital of the Banten Sultanate, 'once a great trading centre in Southeast Asia, especially of pepper'; 'overshadowed by Batavia' by the late 17th century and 'finally annexed to the Dutch East Indies in 1813'; Old Banten continues as a small settlement.

name: Cirebon
why: Wikipedia 'Cirebon': 'the seat of a former Sultanate', founded by Sunan Gunungjati; continues today as a port city of nearly 350,000 (approximate founding).

name: Yogyakarta
why: Wikipedia 'Yogyakarta': 'the capital of the Yogyakarta Sultanate' founded after the 1755 Treaty of Giyanti split Mataram; continues today as a major city and 'the only Indonesian royal city still ruled by a monarchy.'

name: Kediri
why: Wikipedia 'Kediri kingdom': 'a Hindu-Buddhist Javanese kingdom based in East Java from 1042 until 1222'; 'the kingdom's capital is believed to have been established... somewhere near modern Kediri city', which continues today.

name: Singhasari
why: Wikipedia 'Singhasari': 'a Javanese Hindu-Buddhist kingdom located in east Java between 1222 and 1292'; also known as Tumapel; the district of Singosari near Malang continues on the site.

name: Ternate
why: Wikipedia 'Ternate': seat of the Sultanate of Ternate, a major regional power in the pre-colonial spice trade; continues today as North Maluku's largest city (approximate founding date of the sultanate).

name: Tidore
why: Wikipedia 'Tidore': 'in the pre-colonial era, the Sultanate of Tidore was a major regional political and economic power, and a fierce rival of nearby Ternate'; continues today as a city (approximate founding date of the sultanate).

name: Somba Opu
why: Wikipedia 'Fort Somba Opu': 'a fortified commercial center of the Gowa Sultanate... the center of the Gowa Sultanate in the 16th-century until its destruction by the Dutch East India Company in 1669.'

name: Pakuan Pajajaran
why: Wikipedia 'Pakuan Pajajaran': 'the fortified capital city of Sunda Kingdom'; 'settled in at least the 10th century' and made royal capital in the 15th century by Sri Baduga Maharaja; destroyed by Banten in 1579, near the site of modern Bogor.

name: Kutai Kartanegara
why: Wikipedia 'Kutai Kartanegara Regency': seat of the Sultanate of Kutai Kartanegara ing Martadipura; 'the town of Tenggarong is the capital of the regency' today (approximate founding of the sultanate).

name: Malacca
why: Wikipedia 'Malacca City': 'the oldest Malaysian city on the Strait of Malacca... founded in 1396 by Parameswara'; continues today as a heritage city.

name: Johor Lama
why: Wikipedia 'Johor Lama': 'sultan Ali Jalla returned to the Kota Batu area and reestablished the capital at Johor Lama' in the early 1570s; sacked by the Portuguese and Johor's capital moved on; a mukim of the same name continues today.

name: Kedah Tua
why: Wikipedia 'Bujang Valley': 'a sprawling 5th to 14th century CE Indianised Hindu-Buddhist historical complex'; the earliest of the port-kingdoms of Kedah, since abandoned (approximate span).

name: Butuan
why: Wikipedia 'Butuan': 'the former capital of the Rajahnate of Butuan before 1001 until about 1521'; traded 'with places as far as Champa, Ming, Srivijaya, Majapahit, and the Bengali coasts'; continues today as a highly urbanized city.
